leads.text:
If this opinion indicates that it is “FOR PUBLICATION,” it is subject to 
revision until final publication in the Michigan Appeals Reports. 

-1- 
S T A T E O F M I C H I G A N 

C O U R T O F A P P E A L S 

WAYNE COUNTY AIRPORT AUTHORITY, 

 Plaintiff/Counterdefendant-Appellee, 

UNPUBLISHED 
November 03, 2026 
9:14 AM 
v No. 375283 
Wayne Circuit Court 
MICHELLE BALDWIN, 

LC No. 23-001548-CH 
 Defendant/Counterplaintiff-Appellant. 

Before: MURRAY, P.J., and BOONSTRA and RIORDAN, JJ. 

PER CURIAM. 
 Defendant/counterplaintiff Michelle Baldwin appeals as of right the trial court’s order 
granting plaintiff/counterdefendant Wayne County Airport Authority summary disposition under 
MCR 2.116(C)(7) (immunity granted by law) and MCR 2.116(C)(10) (no genuine issue of material 
fact). We affirm. 
I. FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY 
 This case involves the parties’ dispute over certain trees on defendant’s property.1 In 1997, 
defendant acquired real property on Vining Road south of Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County 
Airport. Plaintiff own s land bordering defendant’s property to the north. In 2006, t he Wayne 
County Roads Division closed the road that bisects the two properties at issue, a portion of Vining 
Road, to public access. 
 In July 2016, the Joint Airport Zoning Commission for Wayne and Washtenaw Counties 
approved a zoning ordinance, which regulated “Airport Hazard [s]” within a 20 -mile radius of 
Metro Airport. Joint Airport Zoning Ordinance of Wayne and Washtenaw Counties, § 1.3 and 1.4. 
The ordinance stated: “Structures and trees which project above the height limitations under this 
Ordinance are considered hazards to flying and endanger lives and property.” Id. at § 2.4. The 
ordinance prohibit s “plant[ing] or allow[ing] any tree to grow to a height in excess of the 

1 The record indicates that the property is a few acres and is mostly, or entirely, a wooded area. 
-2- 
limitations prescribed by the terms of this Ordinance . . . .” Id. at § 3.3.2 According to the zoning 
map incorporated by the ordinance , t he height limit for objects in Zone B , which includ es 
defendant’s property, is set at 50 feet above Metro Airport’s elevation. The parties stipulated that 
defendant allowed several trees on her property to grow above the 50-foot height limit. 
Defendant claimed that plaintiff’s employees trespassed on her property multiple times 
from 2018 to 2022 and cut down between 8 and 11 trees. According to Joseph McCabe, plaintiff’s 
representative, plaintiff’s employees removed at least one tree that exceeded the height limit from 
defendant’s property.3 In addition, plaintiff’s contractors performed obstruction surveys of the land 
surrounding Metro Airport in 2018, 2021, and 2022 , respectively . In February 2022, McCabe 
notified defendant that eight trees exceeded the ordinance height limit and were airport hazards. 
Defendant declined McCabe’s offer to remove the trees in May 2022. McCabe said that plaintiff 
offered defendant compensation, although he was not sure of the amount, while defendant denied 
that McCabe offered compensation. 
 Plaintiff filed its complaint against defendant in February 2023, alleging that the 2021 
survey identified 10 trees on defendant’s property that exceeded the height limit. Plaintiff asserted 
that the trees were a public nuisance and requested an injunction requiring defendant to remove or 
trim the trees , or allow plaintiff to enter her property to do so. Defendant filed a counterc laim, 
alleging that the zoning ordinance interfered with the use of her property and was a regulatory 
taking that required just compensation (Count I) . She also alleged that plaintiff’s employees 
entered her property without permission and cut down or trimmed certain trees, entitling her to 
treble damages under MCL 600.2919 (Count III).4 
Plaintiff moved for summary disposition under MCR 2.116(C)(7) and MCR 2.116(C)(10). 
Plaintiff argued that no regulatory taking occurred because defendant created a public nuisance by 
allowing her trees to exceed the height limit , and because its actions did not interfere with 
defendant’s use of her property. Thus, plaintiff contended, it was entitled to summary disposition 
of Count I. Further, with regard to Count III, plaintiff argued that governmental immunity barred 
defendant’s timber-trespass claim because trimming or removing the trees on her property was a 
governmental function. Finally, plaintiff again requested that the trial court enter an injunction 
requiring defendant to comply with the 50 -foot height limit or allowing plaintiff to enter her 
property to ensure compliance. 
 The trial court granted plaintiff’s motion for summary disposition and dismissed 
defendant’s counterclaim. Regarding Count I, the regulatory-taking claim, the trial court ruled that 
the trees that exceeded the height limit were a public nuisance, and abating the nuisance was not a 
taking of defendant’s property. The trial court also ruled that plaintiff did not deny defendant 
productive use of her property, adding that “this Court has no way of determining what adequate 
compensation for the trimming of trees below the 50 foot height restriction would be.” The trial 

2 The ordinance authorizes plaintiff to file an action to abate any zoning violation. Id. at § 6.4. 
3 McCabe asserted during his deposition for this case that plaintiff did not know its employees 
were on defendant’s property at that time. 
4 Count II is not relevant to this appeal. 
-3- 
court further ruled that since the Wayne County Roads Division, not plaintiff, closed Vining Road, 
defendant could not seek relief against plaintiff for the closure. Finally, as to Count III, the trial 
court ruled that governmental immunity barred defendant’s claim for timber trespass. Accordingly, 
the trial court entered the requested injunction and closed the case. Defendant moved for 
reconsideration, which the trial court denied. Defendant now appeals. 
II. SUMMARY DISPOSITION—REGULATORY TAKING 
 Defendant primarily argues that the trial court improperly dismissed Count I, her 
regulatory-taking claim, under MCR 2.116(C)(10) because plaintiff cut trees on her property and 
blocked access to her property. Defendant also argues that the trial court erred by granting 
summary disposition in favor of plaintiff under MCR 2.116(C)(10) on the basis that she did not 
show a precise amount of damages. We disagree with both arguments. 
A. STANDARD OF REVIEW 
 “This Court reviews the grant or denial of summary disposition de novo to determine if the 
moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.” Maiden v Rozwood, 461 Mich 109, 118; 
597 NW2d 817 (1999). “A motion under MCR 2.116(C)(10) tests the factual sufficiency of the 
complaint.” Id. at 120. “All well-pleaded allegations are viewed in the light most favorable to the 
nonmoving party unless documentary evidence is provided that contradicts them.” Haksluoto v Mt 
Clemens Regional Med Ctr , 500 Mich 304, 309; 901 NW2d 577 (2017). “Where the proffered 
evidence fails to establish a genuine issue regarding any material fact, the moving party is entitled 
to judgment as a matter of law.” Maiden, 461 Mich at 120. “A genuine issue of material fact exists 
when the record, giving the benefit of reasonable doubt to the opposing party, leaves open an issue 
upon which reasonable minds might differ.” West v Gen Motors Corp , 469 Mich 177, 183; 665 
NW2d 468 (2003). 
This Court reviews issues of statutory and constitutional interpretation de novo. Toll 
Northville LTD v Twp of Northville, 480 Mich 6, 10-11; 743 NW2d 902 (2008). Because municipal 
ordinances are subject to the same rules of interpretation as statutes, this Court also reviews the 
interpretation of an ordinance de novo. Great Lakes Society v Georgetown Charter Twp, 281 Mich 
App 396, 407; 761 NW2d 371 (2008). 
B. DISCUSSION 
“The Takings Clauses of the Michigan and United States Constitutions both prohibit the 
taking of private property for public use without just compensation.” Gym 24/7 Fitness, LLC v 
Mich, 341 Mich App 238, 260; 989 NW2d 844 (2022) (quotation marks and citation omitted). 
“When a governmental taking results from an actual, physical invasion of the property, a reviewing 
court need not apply a case -specific analysis, and the owner should automatically recover for a 
taking of his property.” Ligon v Detroit, 276 Mich App 120, 132; 739 NW2d 900 (2007) (quotation 
marks and citations omitted). “In contrast, a regulatory taking is one in which the government 
effectively takes a person’s property by overburdening it with regulations.” Merkur Steel Supply, 
Inc v Detroit , 261 Mich App 116, 130; 680 NW2d 485 (2004) ( quotation marks and citation 
omitted). 
-4- 
“A categorical taking occurs when there has been a physical invasion of a landowner’s 
property or when a regulatory taking has deprived an owner of all economically and beneficial use 
of the land.” Gym 24/7 Fitness , 341 Mich App at 260 ( citation modified). “Regulatory taking 
claims that do not rise to the level of a categorical taking are governed by the standard set out in 
[Penn Central Trans Co v City of New York, 438 US 104; 98 S Ct 2646; 57 L Ed 2d 631 (1978)].” 
Id. at 260 -261 (quotation marks and citation omitted). Penn Central requires “balancing factors 
such as the economic impact of the regulation, its interference with reasonable investment-backed 
expectations, and the character of the government action.” Cedar Point Nursery v Hassid, 594 US 
139, 148; 141 S Ct 2063; 210 L Ed 2d 369 (2021). 
 In this case, Count I of defendant’s counterclaim alleged a physical invasion and regulatory 
taking of her property, although she styled her claim exclusively as a regulatory -taking claim. 
Defendant alleges that plaintiff’s employees entered her property without permission to cut down 
trees that exceeded the applicable ordinance’s height limit. She also alleged that plaintiff’s 
enforcement of the ordinance denied her productive use of her property. Defendant claims that the 
denial of productive use is an inverse condemnation of her property. “A claim of inverse 
condemnation is a cause of action against a governmental defendant to recover the value of 
property which has been taken even though no formal exercise of the power of eminent domain 
has been attempted by the taking agency.” Mays v Governor of Mich, 506 Mich 157, 173; 954 
NW2d 139 (2020) (citation modified). 
The parties stipulated that defendant allowed about eight trees on her property to exceed 
the ordinance height limit. Defendant and McCabe both acknowledge that plaintiff’s employees 
entered defendant’s property to cut down or remove at least one tree. Regardless of whether we 
categorize this action by plaintiff as an alleged physical invasion or an alleged regulatory taking, 
because of the nuisance present on her property, plaintiff did not take defendant’s property for the 
purposes of the Takings Clauses, and she is not entitled to just compensation. “[B]ecause no 
individual has the right to use his or her property so as to create a nuisance, the State has not taken 
anything when it asserts its power to enjoin a nuisance -like activity.” Ypsilanti Charter Twp v 
Kircher, 281 Mich App 251, 272; 761 NW2d 761 (2008) (citation modified). Thus, compensation 
is not required when a governmental agency diminishes property value by abating a public 
nuisance. Id. 
The use of land that violates a zoning ordinance is a public nuisance. See MCL 125.3407; 
Ansell v Delta Co Planning Comm’n, 332 Mich App 451, 461; 957 NW2d 47 (2020). Further, the 
creation or maintenance of an airport hazard is a public nuisance under MCL 259.441 , which 
provides that “the creation or establishment or maintenance of an airport hazard is a public 
nuisance and an injury to the community served by the airport in question . . . .” Defendant allowed 
certain trees on her property to grow at least 50 feet above

leads.caseName: BECTON, DICKINSON AND COMPANY v. GARY B. WALKER
leads.text:
SECOND DIVISION
DOYLE, P. J.,
MARKLE and WHITAKER, JJ.
NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed. 
https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules
November 3, 2026
In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
A26A1118. BECTON, DICKINSON AND COMPANY, et al. v.
WALKER.
DOYLE, Presiding Judge.
After the jury returned a verdict awarding punitive damages in the second part
of a bifurcated trial in this toxic tort suit filed by Gary Walker against Becton,
Dickinson and Company and C. R. Bard (“the Defendants”), the trial court ordered
a partial retrial.1 This Court granted the Defendants’ interlocutory application, and
they appeal, challenging the partial retrial and enumerating several errors regarding
1 Oral argument of this case occurred on May 14, 2026, and a recording is
available at https://vimeo.com/1193444896. Dr. Lisa Miller, The Georgia Trial
Lawyers Association, The Advanced Medical Technology Association, The Georgia
Defense Lawyers Association, and The Products Liability Advisory Council, Inc., filed
amicus briefs in this appeal. 
the underlying trial. For the reasons that follow, we affirm the trial court’s grant of a
partial retrial. The remaining enumerations were waived.
For more than 50 years, the Defendants have operated a medical equipment
sterilization facility, global distribution center, and warehouses in Covington, Georgia
(the “Facilities”).2 The Defendants’ sterilization process uses ethylene oxide
(“EtO”), a chemical that the United States Environmental Protection Agency
(“EPA”) and others have determined to be carcinogenic in humans. Between 1970
and 1999, Walker worked as a truck driver in the Covington area, transporting material
(including loading and unloading material) to and from the Defendants’ Facilities
almost daily. Walker also lived within a two-mile radius of the Facilities between 1991
and 2017. 
2 The record in this case is large. It spans 175 volumes and includes over 78,000
pages. As this Court previously has explained, we “will not ‘cull the record on behalf
of a party, particularly in a case such as this where the record is voluminous.’” Pneumo
Abex, LLC v. Long, 357 Ga. App. 17 n.3 (849 SE2d 746) (2020). “‘[I]f we have missed
something in the record or misconstrued an argument, the responsibility rests with
[the Defendants’] counsel.’” Id. We also remind counsel that “[r]eference to an
electronic record should be indicated by the volume number of the electronic record
and the PDF page number within that volume (Vol. Number - PDF Page Number; for
example, V2-46).” Ga. Ct. App. R. 25(d)(2). 
2
In 2017, Walker was diagnosed with diffuse large b-cell lymphoma
(“DLBCL”), which he contended was the result of his exposure to EtO from the
Defendants’ unsafe use of the substance in the Facilities and from fugitive emissions
into the surrounding neighborhood. One of Walker’s experts testified that decades of
exposure to EtO was medically highly likely, simply more likely than not, to be a
meaningful contributing cause of Walker’s DLBCL. After the publication of a news
article in 2019, Walker discovered that EtO was emitted in high quantities from the
Facilities, and he sued the Defendants in November 2021, alleging claims of
negligence and nuisance, and requesting compensatory and punitive damages. 
The Defendants requested a bifurcated trial, which commenced on April 14,
2025. At the end of the liability phase, the jury returned a special verdict in favor of
Walker, explicitly finding the Defendants committed negligence and created a
nuisance, awarding him $20 million in compensatory damages, and finding that
punitive damages were due to be awarded (“Phase I”). The foreperson delivered the
signed and dated verdict to the court and announced the decision. 
On May 5, 2025, jury deliberations for the punitive damages phase (“Phase II”)
began, during which the jury sent several questions to the court, specifically about one
3
of the special interrogatories regarding specific intent to cause harm: “Do you find
that the Defendants believed the consequences of their acts were certain, or
substantially certain, to result in harm and still went ahead with their acts?” The
following day, the jury returned to deliberate, but eventually announced that they were
deadlocked on this special interrogatory. The court gave them an Allen charge,3 and
deliberations resumed. 
Later that day, the jury announced they had a verdict, and the foreperson
delivered the signed and dated verdict to the court, announcing that the jury awarded
$50 million in punitive damages to Walker; with regard to the special interrogatories,
the jury found in favor of the Defendants on one, but found against the Defendants on
the second, which had been the subject of the earlier deadlock — whether the
Defendants were substantially certain their acts would cause harm and still acted. The
Defendants requested a poll, during which Juror 1 recanted her unanimity as to the
Phase II verdict. Specifically, in response to the court’s question whether the verdict
was hers, she responded, “Your Honor, I defer to the group. ... We were told to be
unanimous.” The juror stated that she was just trying to be honest, and the court
3 Allen v. United States, 164 US 492 (1896).
4
asked whether she “agreed with this verdict just to get along with everybody else and
get a unanimous verdict?” The juror again responded, “[w]e were told we needed to
be unanimous.” After completing the poll with the remainder of the jurors still
unanimous in their decision, the trial court sent the jury out. Subsequently, the court
called Juror 1 back into the courtroom, where she was asked questions about her
recantation. At that time she explained that her only disagreement was with the
second special interrogatory, and the jury was unanimous as to the amount of punitive
damages it had awarded. 
The trial court initially granted a mistrial as to the entirety of Phase II, but after
briefing and a hearing, the trial court granted a partial mistrial on Phase II and ordered
retrial solely on the issue of specific intent of harm. The court concluded that the
jury’s Phase I verdict was a unanimous verdict of $20 million returned in open court,
valid, final, and separable from the Phase II questions of the amount of punitive
damages and specific intent to cause harm. Next, the court concluded that the first
question of the Phase II verdict, which awarded $50 million in punitive damages, was
also final, valid, unanimous, and severable from the issue of specific intent to cause
harm, which related only to the statutory cap on punitive damages. Finally, the court
5
declined to enter final judgment on the jury’s verdict until retrial and return of a
unanimous decision on the issue of specific intent to cause harm. The trial court
certified that decision for immediate review, and this Court granted the defendant’s
application for interlocutory appeal. 
1. The Defendants first argue that the trial court erred by ordering only a partial
retrial after the juror recanted on her unanimity to the determination of specific intent
to harm. The Defendants contend that full retrial on both liability and punitive
damages is required. We disagree.
This Court reviews a trial court’s ruling on a motion for mistrial for abuse of
discretion, but it reviews legal questions de novo. See Monroe v. State, 315 Ga. 767,
775(2), 784–85(7)(a) (884 SE2d 906) (2023). When we interpret a statute, “we afford
the ... text ‘its plain and ordinary meaning.’” Deal v. Coleman, 294 Ga. 170, 172(1)(a)
(751 SE2d 337) (2013).
“Our common law ... adheres to certain general principles in the correction of
trial errors that affect less than the whole of a judgment.” Martin v. Six Flags Over Ga.
II, L.P., 301 Ga. 323, 337(III) (801 SE2d 24) (2017). Specifically, if 
a judgment is entire and indivisible, it can not be affirmed in part and
reversed in part, but the whole must be set aside if there is reversible
6
error therein. But where a judgment appealed from can be segregated, so
that the correct portions can be separated from the erroneous, the court
will not set aside the entire judgment, but only that portion which is
erroneous.
 Id. at 338(III) (punctuation omitted). See also Swindell v. Swindell, 231 Ga. 167, 168
(200 SE2d 736) (1973) (“[A] trial court or an appellate court, after examining the
record and transcript to determine if the issues are readily divisible, can order a re-trial
only on specified issues in the case that are readily divisible from other issues in the
case that were rightly deci[]ded, free from error.”). “Limiting the scope of retrial to
only those distinct portions of the judgment that are infirm serves the dual objectives
of judicial economy and respect for the jury’s verdict.” Martin, 301 Ga. at 338(III).
See also OCGA § 9-12-4 (“Verdicts ... shall not be avoided unless from necessity.”);
Lyman v. Cellchem Int’l, LLC, 342 Ga. App. 446 (803 SE2d 375) (2017) (holding that
a retrial was required on the issue of punitive damages alone).
Based on the reasoning of Martin, we discern no error in the trial court’s order
granting a partial retrial only on the issue of specific intent to harm. See Martin, 301
Ga. at 338(III). See also Aldworth Co., Inc. v. England, 286 Ga. App. 1, 5(2)(b) (648
SE2d 198) (2007) (remanding for a jury trial solely on the question of specific intent
7
to do harm in the context of a default judgment with insufficient evidence to support
the full default award of $1,000,000). OCGA § 51-12-5.1(d)(1) instructs that “[i]n any
case in which punitive damages are claimed, the trier of fact shall first resolve from the
evidence produced at trial whether an award of punitive damages shall be made.”
Thereafter,
[i]f it is found that punitive damages are to be awarded, the trial shall
immediately be recommenced in order to receive such evidence as is
relevant to a decision regarding what amount of damages will be
sufficient to deter, penalize, or punish the defendant in light of the
circumstances of the case. It shall then be the duty of the trier of fact to
set the amount to be awarded according to subsection (e), (f), or (g) of
this Code section, as applicable. 
OCGA § 51-12-5.1(d)(2). These portions of the verdict have been unanimously
decided by the jury during Phase I and the first portion of Phase II. The only issue that
remains is “to set the amount to be awarded,” pursuant to OCGA § 51-12-5.1(f), (g),
which is the issue of specific intent to harm, the determination of which will result in
either an award of $50 million or a statutory maximum of $250,000, depending on the
verdict of the jury. 
8
The Defendants have presented no convincing reason why the issue of specific
intent to harm cannot be severed and decided separately from the unanimous portions
of the verdict. Compare Martin, 301 Ga. at 338–39(III) (collecting cases); Lyman, 342
Ga. App. at 447–48. OCGA § 51-12-5.1(d)(2) specifically instructs the trier of fact to
make the determination of specific intent after making a determination of the
appropriate amount of punitive damages. See id. And while it may be the case that
much of the evidence will be repeated in this new trial, that evidence would be
repeated to the new jury if a full retrial occurs. 
Like the Court in Martin, we also see no reason why this determination need be
made by the same jury. See Martin, 301 Ga. at 339(III) (“the natural presumption that
a single fact-finder will make the determination of liability, damages sustained, and
apportionment ... is no different than the presumption that a single fact-finder will
make liability and damages determinations in other contexts” where only partial retrial
has occurred). The plain language of the statute may presume the same group of jurors
will make the decision, but nothing in the language requires it. OCGA § 51-12-5.1. Cf.
England, 286 Ga. App. at 5(2)(b). Thus, the trial cour

leads.caseName: SMRE ROSWELL SPE LLC v. MARIO VASQUEZ MELGAR
leads.text:
SECOND DIVISION
 DOYLE, P. J.,
 DAVIS and WHITAKER, JJ.

 NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
 received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
 the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed.
 https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules

 November 3, 2026

In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
 A26A1353, A26A1354, A26A1355. MELGAR et al. v. SMRE Roswell
 SPE, LLC; and vice versa.

 DAVIS, Judge.

 These companion cases arise from three orders from the Gwinnett County

Superior Court granting in part and denying in part a motion for summary judgment

filed by SMRE Roswell SPE, LLC (“SMRE”) on a civil complaint filed by Mario

Melgar, Marco Villeda, and Carla Herrera (“plaintiffs”) following an incident at the

Roswell Creek Apartment complex owned by SMRE. In Case No. A26A1353, the

plaintiffs argue that the trial court erred by granting summary judgment on (1) their

assault and battery claim; (2) their trespass claim; (3) their premises liability claim; (4)

their breach of contract claim; and (5) their punitive damages claim and Herrera’s
 attorney fees claim. In Case Nos. A26A1354 and A26A1355, SMRE argues that the

trial court erred by denying summary judgment on the plaintiffs’ false imprisonment

claim. For the reasons that follow, in Case No. A26A1353, we reverse the trial court’s

order granting summary judgment on the assault claim as to Melgar, but affirm as to

Villeda and Herrera; and we affirm the trial court’s order on the battery claim as to all

plaintiffs. We also affirm the trial court’s order granting summary judgment on the

trespass claim as to all plaintiffs and the negligence as a result of breach of contract

claim as to all plaintiffs. And we reverse the trial court’s grant of summary judgment

on the premises liability claim as to Melgar and Villeda and remand with direction. We

affirm the premises liability claim as to Herrera. We also reverse the trial court’s grant

of summary judgment claim as to Melgar’s punitive damages and attorney fees claims;

we affirm the trial court’s grant of summary judgment as to Villeda’s punitive

damages and attorney fees claims and Herrera’s punitive damages and attorney fees

claims. In Case Nos. A26A1354 and A26A1355, we affirm the trial court’s order

denying SMRE’s motion for summary judgment on Melgar and Villeda’s false

imprisonment claim.

 Summary judgment is appropriate when there is no genuine issue of
 material fact and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

 2
  In reviewing the grant or denial of a motion for summary judgment, we
 apply a de novo standard of review, and we view the evidence, and all
 reasonable conclusions and inferences drawn from it, in the light most
 favorable to the nonmovant.

Self v. Local Mech. Networking, Inc., 369 Ga. App. 153, 153 (892 SE2d 578) (2023).

 So viewed, the record shows that Detective Charles Craig, an officer with the

City of Roswell Police Department, began working as a part-time security officer for

Roswell Creek Apartments in May of 2021. The arrangements for Craig’s

employment with the apartment complex were made with the manager of the

complex, Darlene Maisonete. Maisonete instructed Craig that they were looking into

“having more of a police presence” at the complex and to have “a contact ... if they

have any issues on the property.” Maisonete specifically asked Craig to check on the

building that was vacant to make sure there was no one in there who was not supposed

to be in there. In early June of 2022, Craig received a list of the apartments that were

supposed to be vacant. Craig had no set hours to work at the apartment complex, but

was limited to working 30 hours per month. He reported those hours by submitting

a spreadsheet via email to Maisonete and received a paycheck from SMRE. Craig

testified that “it varied” whether he would do his apartment complex work at the

 3
 same time he was on-duty as a police officer but that he did not recall that the Roswell

Police Department had any policy against doing so.

 Around 9:30 or 10:00PM on the night of June 22, 2022, Craig was on duty as

a City of Roswell Police Officer. He received “shift pass down notes”1 that indicated

there had been two incidents listed as burglaries of unoccupied residences at the

Roswell Creek apartment complex. Craig went to the complex to patrol the area and,

using the list provided to him by Maisonete, determined unit 809C, the unit listed in

the shift pass down notes, was a vacant unit. Because there were signs that there may

have been people living inside, Craig used his radio to call for backup, requesting

additional officers to assist.2 Three additional officers responded to assist Craig. The

officers first entered apartment 809C and observed items that indicated people were

living in the apartment, but they did not find anyone inside. Then they went to a unit

in building 807, which also should have been vacant because the entire building was

 1
 According to Craig, every incident occurring in a 12-hour shift that is assigned
a case number is sent to all the Roswell Police Officers so that every officer knows
what has transpired in previous shifts.
 2
 It was not unusual for Craig to call for backup assistance from other officers
while he was working at the apartment complex if there was an incident that required
it.
 4
 condemned. Finally, the officers went to apartment 805C, which Craig mistakenly

believed was still part of the 807 condemned building and, thus, he presumed it should

have been vacant.

 Craig and the other officers were all uniformed and had their service weapons

with them as they approached apartment 805C that night. Craig testified that the

Roswell Police Department Glock handguns had flashlights on them, and he believed

the officer in front was using the flashlight on his gun when clearing the buildings.

When asked if he drew his gun that night, Craig responded, “I don’t recall. Yes, I

have [sic] because when we cleared the other buildings. I would’ve had my gun drawn

when we cleared the vacant building. I would’ve had my – for building clearing, I

would’ve had my gun drawn.”

 Craig testified that he stayed five or ten feet behind the other officers as they

went in to clear the unit, but he did not enter the apartment. Upon entering the

apartment, the other officers encountered Melgar, removed him from the building,

and placed him in handcuffs. One of the officers noticed the air conditioner was

running, the lights were on, and there was furniture inside the unit, and he suggested

Craig double-check the list to make sure this unit was supposed to be vacant. Craig

 5
 recalled that one of the other officers asked him, “what we were out there for.” He

checked the list, saw that apartment 805C was rented to Carla Herrera, but still told

the other officers that the apartment was on the vacant list. Rather than admitting

805C was not on the vacant list, Craig pretended to make a phone call to the property

manager. While Craig was on the pretend phone call, Marco Villeda, a second resident

of the apartment, arrived home, and the other officers detained him as well.

Ultimately, Craig directed the residents to be released and informed the residents they

had been removed because of incorrect information on a vacant apartment list.3

 Following the incident, Craig submitted an invoice to Maisonete and was paid

for working at the apartment complex on June 22, 2022, from 9:30PM to 11:00PM,

during the time the incident occurred. Craig also spoke with Maisonete the next day

to tell her the complex needed to repair the side of apartment 805C because it looked

like there had been a forced entry. Shortly thereafter, Craig went on vacation, and

while he was away, he was notified that the Roswell Police Department was

conducting an internal investigation into the incident. Craig resigned from the Roswell

 3
 Neither Melgar nor Villeda spoke English, and none of the officers on the
scene spoke Spanish; the officers used Language Line, a telephone interpreter service,
to convey this information to Melgar and Villeda.
 6
 Police Department in lieu of termination. Although he was not terminated from his

part-time work at the apartment complex, Craig believed that because he was no

longer a law enforcement officer he could no longer remain employed with the

apartment complex.

 Melgar, Villeda, and Herrera filed a complaint against SMRE as owners of the

apartment complex alleging the following claims: (1) assault and battery; (2) false

imprisonment; (3) trespass; (4) negligence arising from breach of contract; and (5)

premises liability under OCGA § 51-3-1.4 They also requested punitive damages and

attorney fees. SMRE moved for summary judgment and following a hearing,5 the trial

court entered an order denying the motion in part and granting it in part. Specifically,

the trial court granted summary judgment as to the assault and battery, trespass, and

premises liability claims. As to the false imprisonment claim, the trial court denied

summary judgment as to Melgar and Villeda but granted it as to Herrera. The trial

court found that the negligence arising from breach of contract was not part of the

 4
 The complaint also named Charles Craig, John Does 1-5, and Corporations A-
E as additional defendants. The parties entered a consent order dismissing the claims
against Craig with prejudice.
 5
 The transcript from this hearing is not in the record before us.
 7
 motion for summary judgment and did not rule on that claim. The trial court also

denied summary judgment as to the attorney fees and punitive damages claims. Both

parties filed motions for reconsideration. On November 26, 2025, the trial court

entered an order denying SMRE’s motion for reconsideration of the false

imprisonment claim and denying the plaintiffs’ motion for reconsideration of the

assault and battery claims. The trial court, however, also granted summary judgment

on the negligence arising from breach of contract claim,6 and on the attorney fees as

to Herrera only, and granted summary judgment on all plaintiffs’ claims for punitive

damages. Both parties appealed the trial court’s orders.7

 Case No. A26A1353

 6
 The trial court’s order on reconsideration explicitly granted SMRE’s motion
for summary judgment on the negligence arising from breach of contract claim as to
Melgar and Villeda, but did not mention Herrera. On December 9, 2025, the trial
court entered an amended order clarifying that summary judgment was also granted
on this claim as to Herrera.
 7
 SMRE initially filed an application for interlocutory appeal of the trial court’s
order. At the same time, the plaintiffs filed a notice of appeal of the trial court’s
orders, SMRE filed a cross appeal from the plaintiffs’ notice of appeal, and we
ultimately granted SMRE’s application for interlocutory appeal. Thus, SMRE filed
identical briefs in A26A1354 and A26A1355.
 8
  1. In the plaintiffs’ first enumeration of error, they argue that the trial court

erred in granting summary judgment and determining that no genuine issue of

material fact exists on SMRE’s liability on their assault and battery claims. We agree

in part and reverse the grant of summary judgment on the assault claim as to Melgar,

but affirm as to the remaining plaintiffs. We affirm the grant of summary judgment on

the battery claim as to all plaintiffs.

 Prior to addressing Plaintiffs’ claims for assault and battery it is important to

recognize the distinction between the two claims. “Any violent injury or illegal

attempt to commit a physical injury upon a person is a tort for which damages may be

recovered.” OCGA § 51-1-14. Although both assault and battery are defined in OCGA

§ 51-1-14, they are recognized as two separate torts. “An assault may be committed

without actually touching, or striking, or doing bodily harm, to the person of another.”

Wallace v. Stringer, 250 Ga.

leads.caseName: Stodden v. Coles County Board
leads.text:
1 

2026 IL App (5th) 250744-U 
NO. 5-25-0744 
IN THE 
APPELLATE COURT OF ILLINOIS 
FIFTH DISTRICT 
______________________________________________________________________________ 

CHARLES STODDEN, ) Appe al from the 
 ) Circuit Court of 
 Plaintiff-Appellant, ) Coles County. 
 ) 
v. ) No. 21- MR-70 
 ) 
COLES COUNTY BOARD and ) 
ROBERT D. BECKER, ) Honorable 
 ) Charles C. Hall, 
Defendants-Appellees. ) Judge, presiding. 
______________________________________________________________________________ 

 PRESIDING JUSTICE CATES delivered the judgment of the court. 
 Justices Hackett and Clarke concurred in the judgment. 

 ORDER 

¶ 1 Held: The plaintiff lacked standing to pursue a claim against the defendants. 
¶ 2 The plaintiff, Charles Stodden, appeals the decision of the circuit court that denied his 
motion for summary judgment and grant ed the defendant’s cross-motion for summary judgment. 
The defendants claim that the plaintiff lacked standing to bring his cause of action . For the 
following reasons, we vacate with directions. 
¶ 3 I. BACKGROUND 
¶ 4 In 2015, the Coles County Supervisor of Assessments , Karen Biddle, was tasked with 
updating assessments for commercial properties in Coles County. The commercial property 
assessments were outdated because the prior assessments were completed in the 1980s. Biddle had 
NOTICE 
This order was filed under 
Supreme Court Rule 23 and is 
not precedent except in the 
limited circumstances allowed 
under Rule 23(e)(1). 
NOTICE 
Decision filed 11/03/26. The 
text of this decision may be 
changed or corrected prior to 
the filing of a Petition for 
Rehearing or the disposition of 
the same. 
2 

informed the Coles County Board (the Board) that she was understaffed and unable to complete 
the reassessment project. Robert Becker , an appraiser, was subsequently hired to update 
commercial property assessments in Coles County. Becker’s last day of employment was 
November 30, 2018, after the commercial property reassessments were completed. 
¶ 5 In 2021, the plaintiff filed a two count complaint, asserting he was a resident and taxpayer 
of Coles County, and challenged whether the hiring of Becker was authorized under Illinois law 
citing article 3 of the Property Tax Code (Code) (35 ILCS 200/art. 3 et seq. (West 2020)). In count 
I, the plaintiff sought a declaratory judgment alleging that the Board illegally outsourced the duties 
of the Coles County Supervisor of A ssessments, a public office , by entering into an ultra vires 
contract with Becker, a private assessor, to update the commercial property assessments in Coles 
County. The complaint alleged, in count II, that board members were illegally compensated 
through optional health insurance benefits. 
¶ 6 The defendants filed a motion to dismiss and argued that the plaintiff c ould not maintain 
his cause of action because he lacked standing; the suit was barred by an affirmative matter 
defeating the claims; there was no actual controversy; the suit was moot; the suit was barred by 
the doctrine of laches; and the plaintiff failed to state a cause of action. On April 25, 2022, the 
circuit court dismissed count II of the complaint finding that the plaintiff had failed to state a claim 
upon which relief could be granted. The plaintiff does not challenge the dismissal of count II on 
appeal. 
¶ 7 During the course of the proceedings the parties conducted discovery depositions of the 
plaintiff, Biddle, Becker, and Stanley Metzger, a Coles County Board member . During the 
plaintiff’s deposition, he was asked about any ownership interest he had in real property located 
in Coles County. The plaintiff was unable to provide any details regarding his ownership interests 
3 

in property located in Coles County. In fact, his attorney admitted, on behalf of the plaintiff, that 
this lawsuit was “brought by him in an individual capacity as taxpayer.” 
¶ 8 On October 27, 2023, the plaintiff filed a motion for summary judgment and argued that 
the Board directly hired Becker upon the recommendation of the Coles County Office and Rules 
Committee. The Office and Rules Committee overse es the Coles County Supervisor of 
Assessments Department. By directly hiring Becker to perform the duties of the position of the 
Coles County Supervisor of Assessments, the plaintiff claimed the Board exceeded its statutory 
authority. Biddle allegedly failed to properly request the necessary budgetary increase and 
approval to hire an employee. Instead, an employee was allegedly hired to fulfill a duty that had 
already been delegated to that office. The plaintiff requested a declaration that the contract between 
the Coles County Board and Becker wherein Becker was retained to perform the statutory duties 
of the Coles County Supervisor of Assessments was ultra vires and void. The plaintiff attached 
discovery depositions of Biddle, Becker, and Metzger along with additional exhibits related to the 
hiring process and the compensation of Becker. 
¶ 9 The defendants filed a cross-motion for summary judgment and response to the plaintiff’s 
motion for summary judgment . The defendants asserted undisputed material facts including that 
the plaintiff did not own real property in Coles County nor did he pay real property taxes in Coles 
County. The plaintiff’s deposition was attached to the motion as an exhibit in support of these 
undisputed facts. In addition to the plaintiff’s deposition, the defendants attached an affidavit of 
Biddle to their motion. Biddle averred that she appointed Becker as a deputy assessor ; no 
contractual documents were signed between she and Becker; Becker signed an oath of employment 
as a deputy assessor on June 1, 2016; and that Becker worked as a deputy assessor under Biddle’s 
direction and control. The official oath signed by Becker was also attached to the motion and 
4 

included Becker’s commitment that he would “faithfully discharge all the duties of the position of 
Deputy Assessor of Coles County, Illinois.” 
¶ 10 The defendants argued that plaintiff lacked standing when he brought the action, in his 
individual capacity, as “ a taxpayer” in Coles County when he revealed in his deposition that he 
did not own real property in Coles County. Because taxpayer standing was a narrow doctrine that 
permitted taxpayers the ability to challenge the misappropriation of public funds, the plaintiff 
lacked standing to bring a declaratory judgment action against the defendants . The defendants’ 
motion for summary judgment additionally included that the plaintiff’s claim was barred by the 
doctrine of laches; the claim was moot; and the claim was an effort to obtain an advisory opinion 
for anticipated future litigation. 
¶ 11 The defendants additionally responded that the evidence demonstrated that the Board did 
not illegally enter into an ultra vires contract with Becker. Rather, Becker was a deputy assessor 
under Biddle and compensated from the budget allocated to her office. 
¶ 12 During the motion hearing on the cross -motions for summary judgment, t he defendants 
argued that the plaintiff did not have standing because he could not provide any detail regarding 
his ownership interest of real property located in Coles County. The circuit court took the matter 
under advisement and subsequently entered a judgment that denied the plaintiff’s motion for 
summary judgment and granted the defendants’ cross-motion for summary judgment. The written 
judgment included that the circuit court reviewed the oral argument of counsel, pleadings, 
affidavits, depositions filed, and the cross-motions for summary judgment. The judgment included 
that it was undisputed that the plaintiff did not own real property in Coles County and did not pay 
real estate taxes in Coles County. The circuit court found that Biddle was involved in the hiring 
process for Becker. Biddle had advised the Board that she was unable to perform the statutorily 
5 

imposed duties that required the reassessment of commercial properties in Coles County and 
initiated the process of hiring an employee. The Board arranged for bids, through a committee, for 
a person qualified to reassess commercial properties. Biddle acquiesced in the hiring process 
giving deference to the committee and then agreed to hire Becker. Funds allocated by the Board 
to the assessor’s office were used to compensate Becker. The Board and Becker never entered into 
a written contract. Rather, Becker signed an appraiser’s oath that was presented to him by Biddle 
to work as an appraiser in Coles County. As such, the circuit court found that process that led to 
Becker’s hiring had not exceeded the statutory authority of the Board or the Assessor and did not 
constitute an illegal, ultra vires act. 
¶ 13 The circuit court had considered and rejected the defendants’ argument that the plaintiff 
lacked standing. The circuit court found that the plaintiff did not own real estate in Coles County 
in his individual capacity, but he was the trustee of a land trust that held title to real estate, and the 
land trust paid real estate taxes in Coles County. The circuit court additionally found that t he 
plaintiff resided and voted in Coles County. For those reasons, the circuit court found that the 
plaintiff had standing to bring his lawsuit for declaratory judgment. 
¶ 14 The plaintiff filed a motion to reconsider the circuit court’s decision and argued that the 
Board did not have the authority to privately contract with Becker. The plaintiff relied on Ashton 
v. Cook, 384 Ill. 287 (1943) and argued that the circuit court’s attempt to distinguish this case from 
the ruling in Ashton was in error. Ashton, as argued by the plaintiff, held that when the constitution 
created an office, no person or board ha d the authority to contract with private individuals to 
expend public funds to perform the duties that were imposed on such officers. See Ashton, 384 Ill. 
287 at 300. The plaintiff argued that since the office of assessor was created by article VII of the 
Illinois Constitution , t he Committee and the Board did not have the authority to hire Becker. 
6 

Biddle’s acquiescence in the hiring of Becker was irrelevant because the hiring procedures were 
disregarded by the Board. Biddle could have requested a budget increase to hire additional 
employees, but she failed to do so. 
¶ 15 In response to the plaintiff’s motion to reconsider, the defendants argued that the Board 
had not entered into an ultra vires contract with Becker where no executed contract between the 
Board and Becker existed. Therefore, there could be no ultra vires contract where there was no 
executed contract. Becker had been hired as a deputy assessor and signed an oath of office for the 
position of deputy assessor on June 1, 2016. The Board had the authority to compensate a deputy 
assessor, and Biddle had the authority to appoint Becker as a deputy assessor under the Code (35 
ILCS 200/1-1 et seq. (West 2024)). Under section 3-40(c) of the Code (35 ILCS 200/3-40(c) (West 
2024)), “each supervisor of assessments may, with the advice and consent of the county board, 
appoint necessary deputies and clerks, their compensation to be fixed by the county board and paid 
by the county.” 35 ILCS 3-40(c) (West 2024). 
¶ 16 The defendants’ response additionally included that the circuit court correctly found that 
Ashton was distinguishable where Ashton involved whether the State’s Attorney had the exclusive 
authority to act as Cook County’s legal advisor. Also, t he Coles County Supervisor of 
Assessments’ position was created by statute, not the constitution. Becker had been hired to assist 
Biddle as a deputy, and he had the specific expertise to perform the assessments. 
¶ 17 The circuit court denied the plaintiff’s motion to reconsider. This appeal followed. 
¶ 18 II. ANALYSIS

Filed 11/2/26
 CERTIFIED FOR PARTIAL PUBLICATION *

IN THE COURT OF APPEAL OF THE STATE OF CALIFORNIA

 SECOND APPELLATE DISTRICT

 DIVISION ONE

 LEE AVILES, B342634, B344966

 Plaintiff and Appellant, (Los Angeles County
 Super. Ct. No. 23STCV08686)
 v.

 NATELA SHENON et al.,

 Defendants and Appellants.

 APPEALS from a judgment and orders of the Superior
Court of Los Angeles County, Barbara Ann Meiers, Judge.
Affirmed as to the judgment. Reversed with directions as to the
orders.
 Stone & Sallus, Jason M. Stone and Elliott Montgomery for
Plaintiff and Appellant Lee Aviles.

 * Pursuant to California Rules of Court, rules 976(b) and
976.1, this opinion is certified for partial publication with the
exception of parts A through E of the Facts and Procedural
Background and part A of the Discussion.
  Grant │ Shenon │ Almaraz, David M. Almaraz and Thomas
Dreblow for Defendants and Appellants Natela Shenon and Yury
Shenon.

 ____________________________

 Yury and Natela Shenon (the Shenons) leased a residential
property to Lee Aviles for approximately two years. At the
conclusion of the tenancy, the Shenons neither returned Aviles’s
security deposit, nor provided him an accounting of how they had
used the funds. A jury found the Shenons had thereby violated
Civil Code section 1950.5, 1 which governs a landlord’s handling
of security deposits under residential leases, and awarded
compensatory damages. The jury further found the Shenons
had acted in bad faith, entitling Aviles to statutory penalties as
well. The Shenons appeal from the resulting judgment. They argue
the court, not the jury, should have decided the issue of bad faith,
and that the evidence supports neither the bad faith finding, nor
the amount of compensatory damages awarded. We disagree and
affirm the judgment.
 Aviles challenges two postjudgment orders: one limiting
his recovery of costs to $1,000, the other denying his request
for attorney fees. The court based both orders on a provision in
the lease that permits a party prevailing in litigation to recover
a maximum combined total of $1,000 in costs and attorney fees
(the fees and costs provision). Aviles argues this provision is
unconscionable and thus unenforceable. He also argues it is void
under section 1953, because it limits procedural rights he would

 1 Unless otherwise indicated, all further statutory
references are to the Civil Code.

 2
 otherwise enjoy in litigation regarding a residential lease. (See
§ 1953, subd. (a) & (a)(4) [deeming “void as contrary to public
policy” any residential lease provision “by which the lessee agrees to
modify or waive” “[h]is procedural rights in litigation in any action
involving his rights and obligations as a tenant”].) In the published
portion of our opinion, we agree with Aviles that the Code of Civil
Procedure section 1032, subdivision (b) right to prevailing party
costs is procedural. Accordingly, the fees and costs provision is void
as it applies to costs. But Aviles identifies no right—procedural
or otherwise—to collect attorney fees, other than the very lease
provision he contends is unenforceable and void. Accordingly, as to
attorney fees, the provision creates a right—rather than abridging
or waiving a right—and does not violate section 1953. For similar
reasons, we need not consider Aviles’s argument that the fees and
costs provision is unconscionable. Striking that provision would not
afford Aviles any relief from the order denying him attorney fees,
because it would leave him without any basis for recovering such
fees.
 Accordingly, we reverse the court’s order limiting Aviles’s
recovery of costs to $1,000. If the costs the trial court awards are
less than $1,000, the court may consider attorney fees, provided
that the combined total of costs and attorney fees may not exceed
$1,000.

 FACTUAL AND PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND
 A. The Lease and Aviles’s Tenancy
 Aviles entered into a one-year agreement with Natela2
to lease a home the Shenons own in Los Angeles (the property)

 2 To avoid confusion, we refer to Natela Shenon and Yury
Shenon by their first names. No disrespect is thereby intended.

 3
 for $9,750 per month (the lease). The lease required Aviles to pay
a security deposit of $19,500.00. It included an option to extend
the lease term for a second year at an increased rent of $10,043
per month. Aviles exercised this option. In November 2022,
he allowed the lease, as extended, to terminate, and moved out.
The parties do not dispute that the Shenons never returned
Aviles’s security deposit.

 B. Aviles’s Complaint and the Shenons’
 Cross-Complaint
 In April 2023, Aviles filed a complaint against the Shenons
alleging they intentionally and wrongfully retained his security
deposit, thereby violating section 1950.5 and breaching the lease
agreement.
 Section 1950.5 places numerous restrictions and
requirements on a landlord’s handling of a security deposit
made under a residential lease (see § 1950.5, subds. (c)-(i)),
and provides the tenant a cause of action if the landlord fails
to comply (id., subd. (o)). It permits a landlord to “claim . . . the
security . . . only those amounts as are reasonably necessary” for
certain enumerated purposes (§ 1950.5, subd. (e)(1)), including
“[t]he repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary
wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of
the tenant.” (§ 1950.5, subd. (b)(2); see also id., subd. (e)(2)(A)
[“[t]he landlord shall not assert a claim against the tenant or the
security for damages to the premises or any defective conditions
that preexisted the tenancy . . . or for the cumulative effects
of ordinary wear and tear occurring during any one or more
tenancies”].)
 “No later than 21 calendar days after the tenant has
vacated the premises, . . . the landlord [must] furnish the

 4
 tenant . . . a copy of an itemized statement indicating the basis
for, and the amount of, any security received and the disposition
of the security, and shall return any remaining portion of the
security to the tenant.” (§ 1950.5, subd. (h)(1).) “[I]f the landlord,
in bad faith, fails to comply with this subdivision [(h)(1) requiring
return of and/or documentation for deductions from the security
deposit],” “[t]he landlord shall not be entitled to claim any
amount of the security.” (§ 1950.5, subd. (h)(7).) “The bad
faith claim or retention by a landlord . . . of the security or any
portion thereof in violation of [section 1950.5]. . . may subject
the landlord . . . to statutory damages of up to twice the amount
of the security, in addition to actual damages.” (§ 1950.5,
subd. (m).)
 The Shenons filed a cross-complaint alleging Aviles had
breached the lease and caused damage to the property exceeding
what the security deposit could compensate them for.

 C. Key Evidence at Trial
 The matter proceeded to a week-long jury trial. The
primary issues at trial were (1) the existence and extent
of damage the Shenons claimed justified their withholding
Aviles’s security deposit—primarily damage to the walls, kitchen
cabinets, and pool coping—and (2) whether this damage predated
Aviles’s tenancy and/or constituted normal wear and tear.

 1. Aviles’s Testimony
 Aviles testified, inter alia, to the following:
 Aviles inspected the property with his real estate agent
before moving in. After the inspection, Aviles exchanged emails
with the Shenons’ real estate agent, in which Aviles identified
items in need of repair. Neither during the inspection, nor in

 5
 these emails did Aviles mention the damage the Shenons would
later cite as the basis for retaining his security deposit. Aviles
did not complete a move-in inspection form documenting the
condition of the property at the outset of his tenancy, as the lease
requires.
 Aviles regularly communicated with Yury regarding the
property. For example, Aviles reported to Yury that a fire alarm
on the property would not stop beeping. At Yury’s suggestion,
Aviles changed the battery, but the beeping continued, and Aviles
removed the alarm from the wall. Aviles reported various other
issues to Yury as well, but never complained about most of the
issues the Shenons would later cite as the basis for retaining his
security deposit.
 Aviles noticed damage throughout the property that he did
not report to Shenon for various reasons. He noticed that a brick
around the pool was “previously cracked, and it chipped or fell
in” but did not complain about it, because he “never used the
pool.” The front doorknob and lock “used to always give [them]
problems,” only some of which he reported to the Shenons, and
the front door had scuff marks on it. Aviles also noticed damage
to the window shades when he moved in and problems with the
kitchen pantry.
 Before moving out of the property, Aviles patched up
holes in the wall where he had mounted his television. He hired
movers and agreed they could have several pieces of furniture
Aviles would otherwise have thrown away. Many months later—
after the filing of the instant lawsuit—Aviles learned that the
movers had left one of these items, a large entertainment center,
at the property.

 6
  Yury invited Aviles to participate in a final inspection
of the property, but Aviles was out of town. On November 29,
2022, Yury informed Aviles via text that, during the inspection,
Yury had “identified many areas of the damage throughout the
house. I’m working to get quotes for the repairs and will get
back to you on the estimate and how it affects your deposit.”
 Yury and Aviles spoke on the phone at some point in early
December, but Yury still did not identify any specific types of
damage or provide estimates for repairs. On December 17, 2022
and January 19, 2023, Yury texted Aviles stating that Yury was
still waiting for the repair estimates. He provided no further
details.
 As of March 9, 2023, the Shenons had neither returned any
portion of Aviles’s security deposit, nor identified the nature of
the damage based on which they were withholding the deposit.
Aviles’s attorney wrote to the Shenons formally demanding
return of the deposit. Yury emailed Aviles’s counsel the next
day with the following list of the damages to the property:
“1. Various cabinets/sliders in the kitchen damaged [¶]
2. Cabinet damaged in living room entertainment cabinet area
[¶] 3. Sliding closet door in downstairs guest bedroom damaged
[¶] 4. Walls damaged throughout the house [¶] 5. Unreasonable
number of holes added to walls throughout the house [¶]
6. Pool brick coping broken [¶] 7. Front door damage/front door
handle damage [¶] 8. Front entry [fire] alarm panel removed
[¶] 9. Multiple window shades are damaged and stained
[¶] 10. Renter left various items in the house that need to be
professionally removed[.] [¶] Moreover, [Aviles] attempted
to ‘patch’ holes throughout the house, but due to the poor
workmanship of this, remediation had to be completed.” The

 7
 email states that the security deposit funds had been insufficient
to pay for repairing these damages, but does not attach any
documentation of the repairs or cost.

 2. Yury Testimony
 Yury testified to the damage outlined in his March 10, 2023
email, his efforts to commission repair work, and the cost of that
work. According to Yury, none of this damage existed at the time
Aviles moved in. Throughout Aviles’s tenancy, Aviles regularly
contacted Yury when he had a problem with the property, but
Aviles never complained about any of the damage for which the
Shenons withheld the security deposit.
 On cross-examination, Yury testified that he had not
withheld any portion of the prior tenants’ security deposit.
Rather, to “help them out,” he had permitted those tenants—a
“really nice family,” the father of which lost his job during the
tenancy—to use their security deposit for the last two months’
rent. Yury had the property repainted after the previous tenants
vacated and before Aviles moved in. Yury had personally taken
“staging” photographs of the property as it

RECOMMENDED FOR PUBLICATION 
Pursuant to Sixth Circuit I.O.P. 32.1(b) 

File Name: 26a0295p.06 

UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS 

FOR THE SIXTH CIRCUIT 

SINMIER, LLC, 
Plaintiff-Appellant, 

 v. 

EVEREST INDEMNITY INSURANCE COMPANY; BEARING 
INSURANCE GROUP, LLC, fka Bankers Insurance, 
LLC; EVERSPORTS & ENTERTAINMENT INSURANCE, 
INC., oka Specialty Insurance Group, 
Defendants-Appellees. 
┐

┘ 

No. 25-4018 

Appeal from the United States District Court for the Northern District of Ohio at Toledo. 
No. 3:19-cv-02854—James R. Knepp II, District Judge. 

Argued: October 20, 2026 
Decided and Filed: November 2, 2026 
Before: GIBBONS, SUTTON, and DAVIS, Circuit Judges. 
_________________ 
COUNSEL 
ARGUED: Matthew I. Henzi, ASHERKELLY LAW, PLLC, Southfield, Michigan, for 
Appellant. Daniel F. Gourash, SEELEY SAVIDGE EBERT & GOURASH CO., LLP, 
Westlake, Ohio, for Appellee s Everest Indemnity Insurance Company and EverSports 
& Entertainment Insurance, Inc. R. Christopher Yingling, NICOLA, GUDBRANSON & 
COOPER, LLC, Cleveland, Ohio, for Appellee Bearing Insurance Group. ON BRIEF : 
Matthew I. Henzi, ASHERKELLY LAW, PLLC, Southfield, Michigan, for Appellant. Daniel F. 
Gourash, Robert D. Anderle, Clare C. Moran, SEELEY SAVIDGE EBERT & GOURASH CO., 
LLP, Westlake, Ohio, for Appellee s Everest Indemnity Insurance Company and EverSports 
& Entertainment Insurance, Inc. R. Christopher Yingling, NICOLA, GUDBRANSON & 
COOPER, LLC, Cleveland, Ohio, for Appellee Bearing Insurance Group, LLC. 
> 
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 2 

_________________ 
OPINION 
_________________ 
SUTTON, Circuit Judge. Sinmier, a commercial real estate lender, loaned Vintro Hotels 
and Resorts funds to purchase a resort in Sandusky, Ohio, and recorded a mortgage as security. 
When Vintro defaulted on its obligation, Sinmier discovered that the resort’s insurance policies 
left its mortgagee interest unprotected. Vintro and Sinmier executed a settlement agreement that 
released Vintro’s mortgage debt and transferred a deed in lieu of foreclosure to Maui Sands in 
Sinmier’s name. Because Sinmier still had not recovered all of its original investment, it brought 
this action in its capacity as mortgagee against Vintro’s insurance broker, one of Vintro’s 
insurance providers, and an underwriter. The district court granted summary judgment to the 
defendants. Seeing no error, we affirm. 
I. 
Sinmier is a commercial real estate lender. In 2018, it loaned Vintro Hotels and Resorts, 
a hotel operator, seven million dollars to purchase the Maui Sands Resort and Waterpark in 
Sandusky, Ohio, via an Open -End Mortgage and Security Agreement. Sinmier recorded a 
mortgage on September 7, 2018. 
Obligated by contract to insure the property, Vintro used Bankers, an insurance broker, to 
identify various avenues of coverage. Bankers contacted a wholesale insurance broker to seek 
quotes on Vintro’s behalf. Two insurance companies, Everest and Berkley, entered the picture. 
Both insurance companies eventually proposed policies. 
On August 23, 2018, Berkley issued a policy, but it soon cancelled the policy when 
Vintro did not make a down payment at the proposed closing. Everest likewise issued a policy 
effective August 23, 2018. When the closing failed to occur on time, Everest also cancelled its 
policy and told the wholesale broker it would have to re-write the policy. 
 On October 16, Bankers asked the wholesale broker to obtain a revised policy quote with 
an effective date of October 19, 2018. Everest issued a second policy, but it listed Sinmier only 
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 3 

as an additional insured, not as a mortgagee, under the commercial general liability portion of the 
agreement. This time around, the closing of the sale of Maui Sands occurred as planned. 
 Then came a rough Ohio winter. Located on Lake Erie, Maui Sands suffered. A frozen 
pipe burst and caused major flooding. Two HVAC systems located on the roof froze, and then 
(surprisingly) caught fire, leaving a smoky, humid waterpark. Still more wind -generated and 
cold-related losses mounted at Maui Sands. 
On January 26, 2019, Vintro submitted an insurance claim to Everest. The insurance 
company advanced $350,000 to Vintro while it processed the claim. Vintro and Everest 
ultimately settled Vintro’s policy claim for an additional $775,000 in June 2019. 
 In March 2019, after Vintro defaulted on its loan obligation, Sinmier sued Vintro. See 
Complaint at 3–7, Sinmier, LLC v. Vintro Hotels & Resorts Ohio LLC , No. 19 -cv-705 (N.D. 
Ohio Mar. 29, 2019). Sinmier sought relief based on claims of breach of contract, fraud, and 
intentional misrepresentation, and looked to foreclose on the property. In October 2019, the 
parties settled. 
As part of this settlement agreement, Vintro provided Sinmier a deed in lieu of 
foreclosure to Maui Sands. The deed was “considered payment in full of Vintro’s monetary 
obligations under the Note or Mortgage.” R.119 -1 at 6. In addition, the agreement required 
Vintro and Inderjit Grewal —Vintro’s owner—to pay Sinmier $627,375 within nine months, 
secured by a consent judgment. The deed in lieu of foreclosure noted that Vintro and Grewal 
“will receive a release of liability on the note” as consideration for their conveyance of Maui 
Sands to Sinmier. R.76-1 at 2. 
 After executing the settlement agreement and accepting the deed in lieu of foreclosure, 
Sinmier filed this lawsuit against Bankers, Everest, and EverSports. 

No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 4 

As to Bankers, Sinmier sought relief based on breach of contract as a third -party 
beneficiary, negligence, negligence per se, misrepresentation, and fraud. As to Everest, Sinmier 
sought relief as a third -party beneficiary based on breach of contract and liability for 
EverSports’s negligence as Everest’s agent. As to EverSports, Sinmier sought relief as a third -
party beneficiary based on breach of contract. 
 The district court granted summary judgment to each defendant and entered final 
judgment. 
II. 
We give fresh review to the district court’s summary judgment orders and draw all 
reasonable factual inferences in favor of the non -movant, Sinmier. See Peffer v. Stephens , 880 
F.3d 256, 260, 262 (6th Cir. 2018). All agree that Ohio law governs the case, meaning that we 
must “predict what the Ohio Supreme Court would do if confronted with” this question. Himmel 
v. Ford Motor Co. , 342 F.3d 593, 598 (6th Cir. 2003). In the absence of an on -point Ohio 
Supreme Court decision, we may look to decisions of the Ohio intermediate courts. Lukas v. 
McPeak, 730 F.3d 635, 638 (6th Cir. 2013). 
The key issue on appeal is whether the settlement agreement extinguished Sinmier’s 
insurable mortgagee interest. If the agreement ended that interest, Sinmier has no basis for relief 
because it brought each of these claims in its capacity as a mortgagee. And Sinmier has forfeited 
any argument that its negligence claims exist independently of its mortgagee interest. 
A mortgagee’s insurable interest exists to protect payment of the debt and dissipates 
when the borrower pays the debt or the lender releases it. A mortgage gives rise to an insurable 
interest in a mortgagee—here, Sinmier. See N. Assurance Co. v. Nat’l Guarantee & Fin. Co. , 21 
Ohio Law Abs. 641, 643 (Ct. App. 1936). This interest extends, however, only “to the amount of 
[the] debt.” McDonald v. Black’s Adm’r , 20 Ohio 185, 194 (1851). A mortgage does not etch 
into stone the mortgagee’s insurable interest. When the underlying debt decreases, the 
mortgagee’s insurable interest reduces in tandem. And when the debt ends, the mortgagee’s 
insurable interest ends. Barwick v. State Farm Fire & Cas. Ins. Co. , No. 24526, 2011 -Ohio-
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 5 

5689, ¶¶ 35–36 (Ct. App. Nov. 4, 2011); see also Lee v. Royal Indem. Co. , 108 F.3d 651, 656 
(6th Cir. 1997). 
In Barwick, a bank holding a mortgage purchased the underlying home at a sheriff’s sale 
after a fire loss. 2011-Ohio-5689 ¶ 36. The Ohio Court of Appeals held that the amount the 
bank received in the sale partially extinguished its interest in any insurance proceeds. Id. In 
reaching this conclusion, the court leaned on a Tennessee Supreme Court decision to the same 
effect. See id. ¶¶ 34–36 (discussing Benton Banking Co. v. Tenn. Farmers Mut. Ins. Co. , 906 
S.W.2d 436, 439 (Tenn. 1995)). While “[t]he mortgagee’s interest in the insurance proceeds is 
recognized as security for the payment of the debt,” Benton Banking explained, that reality lasts 
only as long as the debt does. 906 S.W.2d at 439. “[O]nce the debt is paid by some other means, 
any right to the insurance is thereby extinguished.” Id. 
This is not a new idea. What Ohio and Tennessee do in this area matches what other 
States do and indeed turns on a foundational principle of insurance law. See, e.g., Nationwide 
Mut. Fire Ins. Co. v. Wilborn , 279 So.2d 460, 463 (Ala. 1973); Fireman’s Fund Mortg. Corp. v. 
Allstate Ins. Co., 838 P.2d 790, 795 (Alaska 1992) (noting that “most courts have held that a 
subsequent foreclosure by a mortgagee either partially or completely divests the mortgagee of its 
rights under the insurance contract”); Burritt Mut. Sav. Bank of New Britain v. Transamerica Ins. 
Co., 428 A.2d 333, 338 (Conn. 1980); Power Bldg. & Loan Ass’n v. Ajax Fire Ins. Co. , 164 A. 
410, 411 (N.J. 1933) (“[A]fter the foreclosure sale and the satisfaction of the plaintiff’s debt, it 
ceased to have any interest as mortgagee in the premises covered by the policy.”); 5A J. 
Appleman, Insurance Law and Practice § 3403, at 302 (1970) (“[T]he full or partial 
extinguishment of the mortgage debt itself, whether prior to or subsequent to the loss, will 
preclude, to the extent thereof, any recovery on the policy by the mortgagee.”); 5 Couch on 
Insurance 2d §§ 29:75–77 (1960). 
Gauged by this well -established standard, Sinmier extinguished its insurable interest in 
the property when it signed the settlement agreement and accepted a deed to Maui Sands in lieu 
of foreclosure. Vintro, Grewal, and Sinmier agreed that the conveyance “shall be considered 
payment in full of Vintro’s monetary obligations under the Note or Mortgage.” R.119-1 at 6. To 
the same end, the parties agreed that, “[u]pon receipt of the Deed in Lieu of Foreclosure, Sinmier 
No. 25-4018 Sinmier, LLC v. Everest Indemnity Ins. Co., et al. Page 6 

shall fully release Vintro from any liability or responsibility it may have to pay any deficiency 
amount following the sale of Maui Sands, whether by foreclosure sale or otherwise.” R.119 -1 at 
5. In freely and voluntarily ending Vintro’s mortgage debt to it, Sinmier likewise ended its 
insurable interest as a mortgagee. 
That means Sinmier’s claims against Bankers, Everest, and EverSports fail as a matter of 
law. Each claim rises or falls with the existence or absence of a mortgagee interest. Sinmier did 
not possess any other interest in Maui Sands. It was not an owner. It was not an investor. It was 
a “mere creditor, who ha[d] a specific lien on the property for the payment of [its] debts.” Rands 
v. Kendall, 15 Ohio 671, 680 (1846). Release of the mortgage debt “destroy[ed]” its mortgagee 
interest “as to all the world.” Id. Sinmier’s claims all turn on the same proposition: The 
defendants wronged it when they issued insurance policies that came and went without 
protecting its mortgagee interest. In the absence of such an interest, its claims against the 
defendants are not cognizable ones. 
Trying to fend off this conclusion, Sinmier argues that the settlement agreement and the 
deed arrangement created ambiguous, conflicting terms. While the settlement agreement 
purported to fully release Vintro’s mortgage debt obligation, the deed provided that “the 
Mortgage shall
