SECOND DIVISION
 DOYLE, P. J.,
 DAVIS and WHITAKER, JJ.

 NOTICE: Motions for reconsideration must be
 received no later than 4:30 pm on the 10th day after
 the decision was issued to be deemed timely filed.
 https://www.gaappeals.gov/rules

 November 2, 2026

In the Court of Appeals of Georgia
 A26A1562. NALLEY et al. v. CARROLL COUNTY.

 DOYLE, Presiding Judge.

 Clinton Nalley, Amberly Nalley, The Barn at Nalley Properties, LLC, and

Nalley Properties, LLC (collectively, the “Nalleys”) filed a complaint against Carroll

County seeking a declaratory judgment that a conditional use permit (“CUP”)

previously issued for one of their properties automatically extends to cover a different

piece of property that they subsequently acquired. The parties filed cross-motions for

summary judgment, and after a hearing, the trial court granted Carroll County’s

motion and denied the Nalleys’ motion. The Nalleys appealed, arguing that the trial

court erred by denying their motion for summary judgment because (1) the previously

issued CUP extended as a matter of law to the newly acquired piece of property; and
 (2) the Nalleys acquired vested rights by virtue of the County Planner’s purported

assurances that the previously issued CUP would extend to cover the newly acquired

piece of property. For the reasons that follow, we affirm.

 “On appeal from the grant or denial of summary judgment, we conduct a de

novo review, with all reasonable inferences construed in the light most favorable to the

nonmoving party.” Sterling Planet, Inc. v. GRP Holdco, LLC, 374 Ga. App. 754 (913

SE2d 881) (2025) (quotation marks omitted). Additionally, the construction of a

zoning ordinance is a question of law, which we review de novo. See Sprayberry v. Bd.

of Comm’rs. of Putnam County, 366 Ga. App. 810, 810-11 (884 SE2d 429) (2023).

 So viewed, the record reflects that in February 2016, the Nalleys purchased a

15-acre tract of land in Carroll County, on which they currently live. A 2018 plat of

survey divided their 15-acre parcel into two separate parcels — a 5-acre parcel

including a barn as an event venue and a 10-acre parcel on which their home is located.

In June 2019, they applied for a CUP allowing them to use the five-acre parcel as a

special events venue to host weddings and parties. In August 2019, the Carroll County

Board of Commissioners approved the CUP application, allowing use of the property

as a small special events facility.

 Relevant to this appeal, Section 102-4 of Carroll County’s Zoning Code of

 2
 Ordinances provides as follows:

 Conditional use means a use for a particular piece of property that
 may be allowed by the Governing Authority when specifically listed in
 and provided for by this ordinance. A conditional use is subject to such
 restrictive requirements as in the opinion of the Governing Authority
 would be necessary to insure that the use is not detrimental to
 surrounding property. ...

 Special events facility shall mean any place kept, used, maintained,
 advertised, or held out to the public as a place which serves as a location
 for special events including, but not limited to, weddings and receptions,
 ... and other similar parties, receptions, or events. Such facility includes
 privately-owned properties which have existing agricultural structures
 such as barns or outdoor agricultural areas such as lakes, open pastures,
 or fields, where such special events may take place and that can be
 maintained as or converted back to agricultural structures or areas. Such
 facility shall be open only for scheduled, event-based operations. Such
 facility shall not include places of worship or restaurants. No such facility
 shall be closer than 50 feet from a property line. There shall be three
 categories of special events facilities as follows:

 (1) “Small special events facility” shall mean a special event
 facility with a maximum event size of 150 guests and shall be located on
 a minimum parcel size of four acres or larger.

 (2) “Intermediate special events facility” shall mean a special
 event facility with a maximum event size of 250 guests and shall be

 3
  located on a minimum parcel size of 25 acres or larger.

 (3) “Large special events facility” shall mean a special event
 facility with a maximum event size of 500 guests and shall be located on
 a minimum parcel of 50 acres or larger.

 Additionally, Section 102-12.9 of Carroll County’s Zoning Code of Ordinances

sets forth the procedures for determining whether to grant a CUP, including a

requirement that the applicant must submit “a current boundary survey and plat plan

... [or] other similar drawing, sketch, or plans that properly identifies the boundaries

of the planned development[,]” and a public hearing before the Carroll County Board

of Commissioners, which is required to consider 13 specific factors regarding the

potential adverse effects of granting a CUP on the area in which the proposed use will

be located.

 In 2021, the Nalleys became interested in purchasing a neighboring 15.67-acre

property, on which a climate controlled barn is located, for purposes of hosting

weddings and other events. The 15.67-acre property, which is zoned agricultural, is

contiguous with the eastern border of the 10-acre tract on which the Nalleys’

residence is located but is not contiguous to the western 5-acre tract to which the 2019

CUP applies.

 4
  In August 2021, Clint Nalley spoke over the phone with Janet Hyde, the county

planner, regarding the proposed purchase of the 15.67-acre property. Clint testified

that the substance of this conversation was as follows:

 [S]o I then called Janet Hyde at the County and I asked — I told her, I
 said, this is Clint Nalley, Barn at Nalley Properties, and we’re looking at
 purchasing the property next to us and what amendments would need to
 be made in order for us to extend that permit to purchase this property
 and combine the parcel, and she said, none, as long as you stay under the
 25 acres, and that was the end of that conversation.

Clint testified that during this conversation he did not mention to Hyde that the

Nalleys wanted to host weddings and other events on the property. Also in August

2021, Aaron McCullough, a surveyor engaged by the Nalleys, had a phone

conversation with Hyde in which he inquired generally as to the parameters of

expanding a conditional use permit, and Hyde responded that the two situations in

which an existing CUP required modification were “if an existing facility’s property

exceeded 25 acres in aggregate or ... if new buildings were constructed on the

property.”1

 Thereafter, the Nalleys entered into a purchase agreement for the 15.67-acre

 1
 Hyde’s recollection of her conversations with Clint and McCullough was
never preserved via testimony or affidavit, and she passed away during the pendency
of the litigation.
 5
 property. Prior to closing, the Nalleys applied to formally combine the 5-acre property

and the 15.67-acre property into a single parcel. In December 2021, McCullough e-

mailed Hyde a “preliminary reconfiguration”2 of the two properties, informing her

of the Nalleys’ intention to purchase the 15.67-acre property and asking,

“Conceptually, is this approvable?” Hyde responded in the affirmative. On December

15, 2021, the Nalleys closed on their purchase of the 15.67-acre property for $1.2

million. On December 22, 2021, Hyde approved the Nalleys’ application to combine

the parcels, the combined acreage of which now totaled 20.67.3

 In 2022, after expending substantial amounts for improvements of the newly

acquired property, the Nalleys began hosting weddings on the property and

advertising it as a special event venue. Hyde thereafter informed the Nalleys that the

2019 CUP did not extend to the newly acquired property and that the Nalleys would

need to apply for a separate CUP for the property to hold weddings and other such

 2
 The preliminary configuration depicted a 20.67-acre area including the
western 5-acre parcel to which the CUP applied and the yet-to-be-purchased 15.67-
acre parcel to the east of the 10-acre parcel on which the Nalleys lived as Tract I. The
Nalleys’ 10-acre residential property was represented as Tract II. A narrow, L-shaped
strip of land running along the northwest corner and northern border of Tract II
connecting the 5- and 15.67-acre parcels was also depicted.
 3
 The strip of land running along the northwest corner and northern border of
the Nalleys’ 10-acre residential property as depicted in the preliminary configuration
now connected the 5- and 15.67-acre parcels.
 6
 events there. In March 2022, the Nalleys submitted an application for a CUP for the

newly acquired property. In May 2022, the Carroll County Board of Commissioners

denied the application.

 In June 2022, the Nalleys filed a complaint against Carroll County, the Carroll

County Board of Commissioners, and its individual members, in which they petitioned

for a writ of certiorari as to the decision to deny their CUP application and requested

declaratory relief. However, in January 2025, pursuant to State v. Sass Group, LLC,

315 Ga. 893 (885 SE2d 761) (2023), the trial court dismissed the Nalleys’ original

complaint without prejudice because it had named both Carroll County and the

individual members of the Carroll County Board of Commissioners as defendants.

The Nalleys thereafter brought a renewal complaint pursuant to OCGA § 9-2-61(a)

against Carroll County only, in which they sought a declaratory judgment that the

2019 CUP previously applicable to their 5-acre parcel of property automatically

extends to cover the newly acquired 15.67-acre parcel and, alternatively, that Hyde’s

representations regarding the purchase and combination of the new property with the

5-acre parcel resulted in the Nalleys’ vested right to use the new property as a

wedding venue without a CUP.

 Discovery ensued, and eventually the Nalleys and Carroll County filed cross-

 7
 motions for summary judgment. The trial court convened a hearing on the parties’

motions, thereafter entering an order denying the Nalleys’ motion and granting

Carroll County’s motion. In its order, the trial court ruled that Carroll County’s

approval of the Nalleys’ application to combine the 5-acre parcel to which the 2019

CUP applied with the subsequently acquired 15.67-acre parcel did not automatically

extend the 2019 CUP to the subsequently acquired land. Additionally, the trial court

noted that allowing the Nalleys to bypass applicable zoning ordinances in this way

would deprive Carroll County of the opportunity to assess the impact of the proposed

change in land use on the surrounding area. The Nalleys filed an application for

discretionary appeal, which this Court granted, and this appeal followed.

 1. The Nalleys contend that the trial court erred by declining to issue a

declaratory judgment that the 2019 CUP applicable to their 5-acre parcel extends as

a matter of law to cover the newly acquired 15.67-acre parcel. In particular, they argue

that this result should follow from the fact that Carroll County’s zoning code does not

expressly prohibit it. We disagree.

 “[Z]oning ordinances should be strictly construed in favor of the property

owner, and ambiguities in the language of zoning ordinances should be resolved in

favor of the free use of property. At the same time, [this Court] give[s] local

 8
 ordinances a reasonable construction where possible.” Bd. of Comm’rs of Henry

County v. Welch, 253 Ga. 682, 683(1) (324 SE2d 178) (1985) (cleaned up). “[A]ll parts

of an ordinance relating to the same subject matter must be harmonized to reconcile

conflicts, and any section of an ordinance must be construed in relation to the whole

ordinance of which it is part.” SDS Real Prop. Holdings, Ltd. v. City of Brookhaven, 341

Ga. App. 862, 866(1) (802 SE2d 100) (2017) (quotation marks omitted).

 The te

leads.caseName: GAMBILL v. United States
leads.court: United States Court of Federal Claims
leads.text:
In the United States Court of Federal Claims
 No. 25-238L
 (Filed: October 30, 2026)

 )
 MICHAEL GAMBILL, et al., )
 )
 Plaintiffs, )
 )
 v. )
 )
 THE UNITED STATES, )
 )
 Defendant. )
 )

Lindsay S.C. Brinton, Lewis Rice, LLC, St. Louis, MO, for Plaintiffs. With her on the briefs
were Meghan S. Largent, Michael Armstrong, and Marlee L. Rowe.

Kenneth Gordon Long, Senior Attorney, Environmental Enforcement Section, Environment
and Natural Resources Division, United States Department of Justice, Washington, D.C.,
for Defendant. With him on the briefs was Adam R.F. Gustafson, Principal Deputy
Assistant Attorney General, Environment and Natural Resources Division.

 OPINION AND ORDER

SOLOMSON, Chief Judge.

 Ralph Waldo Emerson, in his essay Self-Reliance, offered a line that every
schoolchild half-remembers and every litigant should forget:

 A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds, adored
 by little statesmen and philosophers and divines. With
 consistency a great soul has simply nothing to do. He may as
 well concern himself with his shadow on the wall. Speak
 what you think now in hard words and to-morrow speak

 1
  what to-morrow thinks in hard words again, though it
 contradict every thing you said to-day.

Ralph Waldo Emerson, Self-Reliance, in Essays: First Series 43, 57 (Houghton, Mifflin & Co.
1903). 1 Emerson may be right about the soul. But his advice has no place in the
courtroom. What is liberty for the philosopher is for the litigant a trap. A great thinker
may say one thing today and change his mind tomorrow; a party moving for summary
judgment may not.

 To be clear, this Court takes no issue with pleading legal theories in the alternative
— that is fine — but the facts themselves cannot change depending on a party’s preferred
legal argument. A litigant may not build a summary-judgment motion on one factual
premise, accuse its opponent of admitting that premise, and then try to defeat the
opponent’s motion by denying the same premise. That is precisely what Plaintiffs
attempted here in this Fifth Amendment rails-to-trails takings case. It does not work. On
Plaintiffs’ own summary-judgment record — including what are essentially the parties’
stipulated facts — the railroad acquired the North Carolina rail corridor at issue (the “rail
corridor”) in fee simple, which left Plaintiffs nothing for the government to take.
Plaintiffs lose based on the summary-judgment record they built.

 In Plaintiffs’ “Statement of Uncontroverted Facts” of their motion for partial
summary judgment, Plaintiffs assert that “[i]n late 1894 and early 1895,” the
Hendersonville and Brevard Railway, Telegraph and Telephone Company (“HBR”)
“acquired its rights” to the rail corridor “via conveyances from the owners of the land
over which it built its railroad.” ECF No. 26 (“Pl. MSJ”) at 5, 7. 2 Plaintiffs attached those
“Original Conveyances” (or the “source deeds”) as Exhibit M to their motion, correlated
them to Interstate Commerce Commission (“ICC”) “Valuation Maps” and schedules
(together, the “ICC Valuation Maps”) as Exhibit N, and then matched each Plaintiff to
specific source deeds, ICC Valuation Map parcels, and government responses to
Plaintiffs’ requests for admissions (“RFAs”). Id. at 7–9. Plaintiffs even included a table
depicting the relationships among those evidentiary materials, id. at 8–10, further
asserting that the government had “admitted that the Original Conveyances . . . are the

1 Available at https://archive.org/details/worksofemerson02emeruoft/page/57.

2 Citations to the parties’ briefs and exhibits are to the page numbers printed in the footer of the

documents themselves, where such numbers exist, rather than to the electronic filing system’s
stamped page numbers in the header. Citations to the transcript of the June 24, 2026 oral
argument, ECF No. 36 (“Tr.”), are to page and line.

 2
 relevant conveyances by which HBR acquired its interests in the Corridor.” Id. at 8 n.9.
That record architecture is Plaintiffs’ entire case for summary judgment. It establishes
the identity and location of the rail corridor segments, including the link among Plaintiffs’
modern parcels, the historic rail corridor, and the property interests Plaintiffs allege were
taken without compensation when, on June 29, 2021, the Surface Transportation Board
(“STB”) issued a Notice of Interim Trail Use (“NITU”) preserving the rail corridor for
railbanking and interim use as a recreational trail. 3 But that record does not establish that
Plaintiffs own those rail corridor segments as a matter of law. Ownership turns on what
estate the source deeds conveyed to HBR.

 The government — in its responses to Plaintiffs’ RFAs, in its own motion for
summary judgment, and in its response to Plaintiffs’ summary-judgment motion —
agreed with Plaintiffs regarding the identity of the property segments and how HBR
acquired its interest in the rail corridor, but argues that the conveyances to HBR were in
fee simple as a matter of North Carolina law. See ECF No. 25 (“Def. MSJ”) at 6–9, 11–20;
ECF No. 28 (“Def. Resp.”) at 12 & n.8, 19; ECF No. 26-9 (“Pl. MSJ Ex. I”) at 5–18.

 In opposing the government’s motion, however, Plaintiffs attempt to recast as void
the very same source deeds they relied upon. See ECF No. 27 (“Pl. Resp.”) at 8–10. Their
reply then returned to their opening position: that the source deeds were valid but
conveyed, at most, an easement. ECF No. 31 (“Pl. Rep.”) at 14–16. 4

 North Carolina law forecloses Plaintiffs’ argument that the source deeds provided
HBR with only an easement. According to Plaintiffs’ own motion, relying upon what are
essentially stipulated facts, nine recorded conveyances in the record “give, grant, bargain,
sell, and convey” to HBR “and its successors forever” “a strip of land,” and refer to that
strip as “the land hereby conveyed.” Pl. MSJ at 25–26 (emphasis added). North Carolina
presumes that a conveyance of real estate passes fee-simple title unless the instrument
plainly expresses or makes evident an intent to convey a lesser estate. N.C. Gen. Stat.
§ 39-1. These source deeds do not plainly convey a lesser estate. The Supreme Court of
North Carolina’s decision in McCotter v. Barnes confirms that railroad-purpose language,
a two-dollar consideration, and future location of the precise strip do not transform a

3 The NITU is dated June 28, 2021, and was served on June 29, 2021. Am. Compl. ¶ 7; Pl. MSJ at
12. The parties treat June 29, 2021 as the operative date, and so does this Court.
4 To be precise, Plaintiffs’ opening motion did invoke ambiguity, but only in support of their

argument about the nature of the estate the deeds conveyed. See Pl. MSJ at 23, 29–34; infra Part
V.C.1.

 3
 grant of land into an easement. 247 N.C. 480, 101 S.E.2d 330 (1958). The undersigned
recently applied that same case — construing this very family of deeds — in Penland v.
United States, 183 Fed. Cl. 114 (2026), concurring with Judge Hadji’s reasoning in Bevirt v.
United States, 177 Fed. Cl. 275 (2025), recons. denied, 180 Fed. Cl. 217 (2026) (Hadji, J.), appeal
dismissed per stipulation, No. 26-1703 (Fed. Cir. Oct. 16, 2026). And Judge Bonilla has since
reached the same conclusion for the same deed family on this same corridor. Barry v.
United States, -- Fed. Cl. --, 2026 WL 3213185, at *10–11 (Oct. 23, 2026). This Court once
again adheres to the same reasoning applied in those decisions. Because HBR acquired
the rail corridor in fee simple, Plaintiffs cannot show a genuine dispute of fact that any
interest in the rail corridor descended to Plaintiffs through their claimed chains of title.

 In short, even if Plaintiffs owned land next to the rail corridor on the date of the
NITU — another fact with which the government agrees — they owned neither the rail
corridor nor a reversionary interest in that corridor. The NITU therefore took nothing
from them. Moreover, no substantive rule of property law permits the underlying
acquisition facts to change with the type of estate conveyed. The same documentary
evidence either locates the relevant strips conveyed to the railroad in the 1890s, or it does
not. And whether the located strips passed to HBR in fee or as an easement is a separate
legal question. But Plaintiffs cannot have it both ways: the deeds and ICC Valuation
Maps cannot be reliable enough to locate the rail corridor when Plaintiffs asserted the
deeds at issue conveyed easements, yet are latently ambiguous and void once the
government demonstrated that, as a matter of law, the same deeds conveyed a fee.
Viewed through a procedural lens, Plaintiffs cannot assert that the summary-judgment
record supports two mutually exclusive sets of facts. To be clear, this Court’s primary
holding is that, under North Carolina law, the source deeds conveyed the rail corridor to
HBR in fee simple. That holding alone requires denial of Plaintiffs’ motion. Plaintiffs’
shifting positions matter to the government’s motion, because they explain why Plaintiffs
cannot manufacture a factual dispute to escape that holding’s consequences.

 Accordingly, and for the reasons explained in more detail below, Plaintiffs’ motion
for partial summary judgment, ECF No. 26, is DENIED, and the government’s motion
for summary judgment on title and liability, ECF No. 25, is GRANTED.

I. PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND

 Plaintiffs commenced this action alleging that the STB’s issuance of the NITU
effected a Fifth Amendment taking of their asserted reversionary interests in the rail
corridor. On June 20, 2025, with leave of this Court, ECF No. 10, Plaintiffs filed their still-
operative amended complaint. ECF No. 11 (“Am. Compl.”). The amended complaint

 4
 alleges that the rail corridor was created by easements, that each Plaintiff owned “land
adjacent to” the former railroad right-of-way on the date of the NITU, and that, upon
abandonment, Plaintiffs “would have had the exclusive right to physical ownership,
possession, and use of their property free of the railroad easement.” Am. Compl. ¶¶ 6,
12; id. ¶¶ 15–20.

 Following the close of discovery, the parties filed simultaneous dispositive
motions on December 12, 2025. Plaintiffs moved for partial summary judgment on title
and liability; the government cross-moved for summary judgment on the same issues.
The key question is this: what did Plaintiffs’ predecessors-in-interest convey to the
railroad in 1894 and 1895? Plaintiffs, in their summary-judgment motion, assert that the
source deeds are enforceable instruments by which HBR “acquired its rights to the
Corridor,” but contend that they conveyed mere easements. Pl. MSJ at 7–9, 23–33. As
noted above, the government agrees with Plaintiffs that HBR acquired its rights via the
source deeds but contends that the rail corridor strips were transferred to the railroad in
fee simple — leaving no property interest to revert to adjacent owners. Def. MSJ at 11–
19. Thus, according to the government, Plaintiffs possessed no property interest for the
NITU to take. Id.

 On January 9, 2026, the parties filed simultaneous response briefs. ECF No. 27;
ECF No. 28. On January 28, 2026, each side replied. ECF No. 31; ECF No. 32 (“Def. Rep.”).
On February 6, 2026, the government filed a notice of supplemental authority directing
this Court to Bevirt and attaching the order denying reconsideration in that case. ECF
Nos. 33, 33-1 (Bevirt v. United States, 180 Fed. Cl. 217 (2026) (order denying
reconsideration)).

 This Court held oral argument on June 24, 2026. Tr. 1:16–18.

II. JURISDICTION

 This Court has jurisdiction pursuant to the Tucker Act, which grants this Court
authority “to render judgment upon any claim against the United States founded either
upon the Constitution” or upon federal statutes and regulations. 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1).
A claim that the United States has taken private property without just compensation, in
violation of the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause, is such a claim, and Plaintiffs assert
prec

leads.caseName: Camo Disposal Company, LLC v. Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough, LLP
leads.text:
IN THE COURT OF APPEALS OF TENNESSEE
AT NASHVILLE
July 8, 2026 Session
CAMO DISPOSAL COMPANY, LLC ET AL. v. NELSON MULLINS RILEY 
& SCARBOROUGH, LLP ET AL.
Appeal from the Circuit Court for Davidson County
No. 24C357 Thomas W. Brothers, Judge
___________________________________
No. M2025-01937-COA-R3-CV
___________________________________
This appeal stems from a legal malpractice action involving a failed commercial real estate 
transaction. The plaintiffs alleged that their fo rmer attorneys negligently failed to extend 
a contractual due diligence period, resulting in the loss of a large earnest money deposit.
One plaintiff also asserted that he personally received negligent advice about the risk 
associated with a bridge loan used to fund the deposit. The defendants filed a counterclaim 
for unpaid legal fees. Ultimately, the trial court granted summary judgment to the 
defendants on all claims. The plaintiffs appeal. We affirm.
Tenn. R. App. P. 3 Appeal as of Right; Judgment of the Circuit Court Affirmed; 
Case Remanded
KRISTI M. DAVIS, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which FRANK G. CLEMENT,J R., 
C.J., and ANDY D. BENNETT, J., joined.
Michael E. Richardson, Chattanooga, Tennessee, for the appellants, Camo Disposal 
Company, LLC and Dan Maddox.
James F. Sanders, Nathan C. Sanders, and Satchel R. Fowler, Nashville, Tennessee, for the 
appellees, Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough, LLP and Laurence M. Papel.
OPINION
BACKGROUND
On January 16, 2023 (the “Execution Date”), Camo Disposal Company, LLC 
(“Camo”) entered into a Purchase and Sale Agreement (the “PSA”) whereby it agreed to 
purchase certain real property. At the time, Camo was represented by Laurence Papel, a 
10/30/2026
10/30/2026
-2 -
partner with Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough, LLP (“Nelson Mullins,” together with 
Mr. Papel, “Defendants”), pursuant to a representation agreement executed February 7, 
2022 (the “Engagement Letter”). The Engagement Letter specified that Nelson Mullins
would “represent Camo alone” and would not represent any of Camo’s officers, directors, 
members, or related persons “unless we otherwise agree specifically in writing hereafter.” 
During the time relevant to this appeal, Dan Maddox was Chairman of Camo’s board and 
owned a membership interest in Camo; Stephen Bridges was Camo’s President and a 
member of its board; and Jerry Cover was a founding member of Camo and also a member 
of its board.
The PSA required that Camo pay an initial earnest mone y deposit of $100,000 
within two business days of the Execution Date and an additional earnest money deposit 
of $3,900,000 within forty ‑five days of the Execution Date (these amounts together, the 
“Earnest Money Deposit”). All of this earnest money was to be credited toward the 
purchase price. Under certain conditions, some of this earnest money was refundable, as 
provided in the PSA:
2.3. Refunda ble and Nonrefundable Earnest Money. Except as 
provided below, the Earnest Money Deposit shall remain fully refundable
throughout the Due Diligence Period (defined below). Upon expiration of 
the Due Diligence Period, if Purchaser has not terminated this Agreement 
during the Due Diligence Period, One Million and 00/100 Dollars 
($1,000,000.00) of the Earnest Money Deposit shall become non‑refundable, 
but applicable to the Purchase Price. The remaining Three Million and 
00/100 Dollars ($3,000,000.00) shall remain refundable following the 
expiration of the Due Diligence Period, but only if (i) Seller is unable to 
deliver clear title to the Property or otherwise defaults under this Agreement 
or (ii) Purchaser is unable to obtain both (A) a processing center permit(s) 
from the Tennessee Division of Solid Waste Management necessary to 
operate its business and (B) transfer station operating permit from the 
Tennessee Division of Solid Waste Management (each a “Permit,” and 
together the “Permits,” the obtainment of both Permits being the “Earnest 
Money Refund Conditions”). Should Purchaser not terminate this 
Agreement pursuant to sections (i) or (ii) in this Section 2.3 before the 
Closing Date, the Earnest Money Deposit shall become fully nonrefundable, 
but applicable to the Purchase Price. The above notwithstanding, One 
Hundred Thousand and 00/100 Dollars ($100,000.00) of the Earnest Money 
Deposit shall be non ‑refundable as of the Effective Date, but applicable to 
the Purchase Price, except in the event of Seller’s default hereunder or 
inability to deliver clear title.
The PSA also provided for an initial due diligence period of sixty days from one business 
day following the Execution Date. The due diligence period could be extended for an 
-3 -
additional forty ‑five days “[i]n the event that Purchaser’s Phase I Environmental Site 
Assessment or any other Property related diligence report determines that further testing of 
the Property is required[.]” Accordingly, the initial due diligence period was set to expire 
in March 2023. In the event further testing of the property was required, the due diligence 
period could be extended.
To fund the additional earnest money deposit of $3,900,000, Dan Maddox and his 
father, Jim Maddox, sought a short-term loan (the “Bridge Loan”) from Truxton Trust 
(“Truxton”). On February 9, 2023, Dan Maddox emailed Bryant Tirrill, a Truxton loan 
officer, and proposed a loan structure whereby the Maddoxes would “sign personally” on 
the Bridge Loan. In this scenario, Truxton would make the loan contingent upon Camo 
granting Truxton a power of attorney to “call back the earnest money” if it had not been 
repaid on or before April 28, 2023. Mr. Papel was not copied on this email. 
Mr. Tirrill emailed Mr. Papel about the Bridge Loan on February 14, 2023, and they 
later agreed that Truxton would draft the loan documents except for the Power of Attorney 
and Recognition Agreement giving Truxton the power to withdraw the earnest money (the 
“Clawback Documents”), which Mr. Tirrill asked Mr. Papel to draft. During this exchange, 
Mr. Tirrill assumed that Defendants represented the Maddoxes. Mr. Papel, for his part,
assumed that Camo would be the borrower on th e Bridge Loan. In one email, Mr. Tirrill 
stated to Mr. Papel: “If we have attorney prepare docs and with your knowledge of the 
deal, are you comfortable preparing the docs on behalf of Truxton. I realize there needs to 
be notices as you are Maddox attorney.” On February 27, 2023, Woods Drinkwater, an 
associate with Nelson Mullins, emailed drafts of the Clawback Documents to Mr. Tirrill 
identifying Camo as the borrower of the Bridge Loan and the Maddoxes as guarantors of 
the loan. Mr. Tirrill responded that his understanding was that the Maddoxes were to be 
the borrowers on the loan. In an email to Mr. Drinkwater, Mr. Papel referred to “our 
clients,” plural. 
When the Maddoxes closed on the Bridge Loan on March 2, 2023, Camo was not a
borrower on the loan. Dan Maddox later explained that he chose not to add Camo as a 
borrower due to concerns about a separate potential lawsuit involving Camo. However, 
Dan Maddox executed the Clawback Documents in his capacity as an authorized 
representative of Camo. Meanwhile, Camo’s Board executed a borrowing resolution 
designating Dan Maddox and Mr. Bridges as authorized representatives of Camo and 
approving actions taken in connection with th e Bridge Loan and the PSA, a document 
whose scope and effect later became a point of disagreement between the parties. Camo’s 
amended operating agreement provided that a borrowing resolution needed to be approved 
by its Board of Directors before incurring debt over $500,000. Even still, Camo appears 
nowhere in the loan documents as a borrower.
According to Dan Maddox, he called Mr. Papel prior to closing on the Bridge Loan 
for reassurance that the short-term loan he was getting for Camo would not be at risk. By 
-4 -
Dan Maddox’s account, Mr. Papel told him that there would not be any risk so long as the 
initial due diligence period was extended and assured him that it would be done. 
Conversely, Mr. Papel denies that this convers ation ever took place. Instead, Defendants 
assert that Camo told Mr. Papel that it would handle the environmental diligence but then 
failed to do so and, therefore, never received a report justifying an extension of the 
diligence period. As such, Mr. Papel never attempted to extend the due diligence period.
At some point after the due diligence period expired, the transaction fell apart, and 
Camo terminated the PSA. Truxton was able to recover $3,000,000 of the $3,900,000 it 
loaned the Maddoxes. However, $900,000 of the earnest money had “gone hard” (a phrase 
used in the real estate field meaning that the money became nonrefundable) and was 
forfeited to Fleetco, the intended seller of the property. The Maddoxes then obtained a 
loan from Farm Credit Mid-America (“Farm Credit”) to pay off the $900,000 still owed to 
Truxton. Dan Maddox and Camo (together, “Plaintiffs”) posit that Camo and the 
Maddoxes had a handshake agreement that Camo would reimburse the Maddoxes for this 
money. Nevertheless, Dan Maddox has made all payments toward the Farm Credit loan. 
Notably, Camo’s own financial records later included a footnote recognizing a verbal 
commitment by Camo to reimburse the Maddoxes for funds not recovered but describing 
this commitment as “not a legal liability” of the company.
On February 13, 2024, Plaintiffs filed a Complaint in the Davidson County Circuit 
Court (the “trial court”) alleging among other things that Defendants “were negligent and 
breached the applicable standards of due professional care in failing to obtain an extension 
of the due diligence period” and that Defendants “committed a negligent misrepresentation 
when [Mr.] Papel told [Dan] Maddox that he would get the initial due diligence period 
extended.” The Complaint alleged further that Mr. Papel was representing Dan Maddox 
individually at the time he made his misreprese ntation about the due diligence period. 
Plaintiffs also alleged that they relied on this faulty information and that the failure to

IN THE COURT OF CHANCERY OF THE STATE OF DELAWARE

ACCELERANT TWISTER, LLC, and
ACCELERANT HOLDING, LLC,

 Plaintiffs,
 CONSOLIDATED
 v. C.A. No. 2023-0887-LWW

MARJO, LLC and JOHN T. SULLIVAN,

 Defendants/Counter-Plaintiffs,

 v.

ACCELERANT TWISTER, LLC,
ACCELERANT HOLDING, LLC,
ACCELERANT PARTNERS, LLC,
MICHAEL BOROM, GRANT SCHUSTER,
and ALAN ELLMAN,

 Counter-Defendants.

 MEMORANDUM OPINION

 Date Submitted: July 16, 2026
 Date Decided: October 30, 2026

Richard L. Renck, Mackenzie M. Wrobel, D. Stuart Bartow, & Qingqing Zhang,
DUANE MORRIS LLP, Wilmington, Delaware; Attorneys for Plaintiffs and
Counter-Defendants Accelerant Twister, LLC, and Accelerant Holding, LLC, and
Counter-Defendants Accelerant Partners, LLC, Michael Borom, Grant Schuster,
and Alan Ellman

Victoria K. Petrone & Mark A. Denney, Jr., BROCKSTEDT MANDALAS
FEDERICO LLC, Wilmington, Delaware; Thomas C. Costello & Anne L. Preston,
COSTELLO LAW GROUP, Towson, Maryland; Attorneys for Defendants/Counter-
Plaintiffs Marjo, LLC, and John T. Sullivan

WILL, Vice Chancellor
  This post-trial decision resolves a dispute among the co-founders of

Accelerant Twister, LLC, a company formed to design, build, and commercialize an

automated cannabis cone-rolling machine. In 2019, engineer John T. Sullivan—

acting through his entity, Marjo, LLC—joined with Michael Borom, Grant Schuster,

and Alan Ellman to bring Sullivan’s machine concept to market. Marjo licensed its

intellectual property and agreed to provide consulting services to Twister in

exchange for milestone payments and a 15% non-dilutable membership interest.

 Early optimism soon gave way to engineering setbacks, mounting capital

needs, and regret over Marjo’s anti-dilution protection. In 2021, Borom, Schuster,

and Ellman formed a new entity—Accelerant Holding, LLC—into which every

Twister member except Marjo exchanged its equity. From then on, the three

founders raised capital at the Holding level by touting Twister’s machines and

business model. They used those funds both to lend money back to Twister at 25%

interest and to develop new product lines inside Holding. Twister later terminated

the license agreement and refused to pay Marjo the $1 million minimum payment.

This litigation followed.

 The parties have asserted numerous contract, governance, and tort claims

against one another. After trial, neither side emerges unscathed.

 On the contract and governance claims, Marjo largely prevails. The license

agreement is valid and enforceable, and Twister breached it by failing to pay Marjo

 1
 the final $1 million milestone. Marjo is entitled to $1 million in damages plus

contractual interest and the return of the early prototype, demonstration unit, and

original drawings. Marjo’s related demand for Twister’s commercial machines,

along with the patent-ownership portion of Twister and Holding’s declaratory

judgment claim, is dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Under Twister’s

limited liability company agreement, the managers validly approved the July 2021

unit exchange in which Holding acquired 83.7% of Twister. Yet Twister entered

into a 25% revolving credit agreement and an intercompany services agreement with

Holding without the required member vote. For their part, Marjo and Sullivan

breached the agreement’s confidentiality provision by forwarding internal company

information to third parties, warranting nominal damages.

 On the fiduciary duty claims, the outcome is likewise mixed. Acting as a

conflicted majority of Twister’s board of managers, Borom, Schuster, and Ellman

breached their duty of loyalty—aided and abetted by Holding—by charging Twister

an unfair 25% interest rate under the revolving credit agreement and by usurping

Twister’s capital-raising opportunities to build separate product lines in Holding.

Because an entity-level recovery would return most of the funds to Holding and the

breaching parties, Marjo is awarded direct, pro rata damages of $43,142.46 for the

interest overcharge and $462,000 for the usurped opportunities. By contrast,

 2
 Twister’s guaranty of Holding’s credit line was fair, and Twister and Holding’s

reciprocal fiduciary duty claim against Sullivan fails.

 Finally, the parties’ peripheral claims and fee-shifting requests are rejected.

Twister and Holding’s conversion claim over software source code is preempted by

the federal Copyright Act. And Marjo’s claim for breach of a consulting agreement

is defeated by the contract’s plain terms. Each side will bear its own fees and costs.

I. BACKGROUND

 Unless otherwise noted, the following facts were stipulated to by the parties

or proven by a preponderance of the evidence at trial.1

 A. The Cone-Rolling Machine

 John T. Sullivan is a commercial equipment inventor and designer with a

background in electrical engineering.2 He is the managing member of Marjo, LLC,

a Maryland limited liability company he formed.3

 NO. CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX

 IN THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS

 OF THE STATE OF HAWAI#I

 CLAUDIA ROHR, Plaintiff-Appellant, v.
 COUNTY OF HAWAI#I PLANNING DEPARTMENT; HUI HO#OLEIMALUO; and
 KA #UMEKE KA#EO PCS, Defendants-Appellees

 APPEAL FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE THIRD CIRCUIT
 (CIVIL NO. 3CCV-XX-XXXXXXX)

 SUMMARY DISPOSITION ORDER
 (By: Nakasone, Chief Judge, Leonard and Guidry, JJ.)
 Self-represented Plaintiff-Appellant Claudia Rohr

(Rohr) appeals from the April 1, 2024 Final Judgment (Judgment),

entered by the Circuit Court of the Third Circuit (Circuit

Court).1 Rohr also challenges the Circuit Court's March 3, 2023

Order Granting Defendant[-Appellee] County of Hawai#i Planning

Department's [(Planning Department's)] Motion to Dismiss

Complaint, Filed on November 18, 2022; March 3, 2023 Order

Granting Defendant[-Appellee] Hui Ho#oleimaluō's [(Hui's)] Motion

to Dismiss and Substantive Joinder in [the Planning Department's]

Motion to Dismiss Complaint, Filed November 21, 2022; March 3,

2023 Order Granting Defendant[-Appellee] Ka #Umeke K[ā]#eo PCS

 1
 The Honorable Henry T. Nakamoto presided.
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

(Charter School's) Substantive Joinder in [the Planning

Department's] Motion to Dismiss Complaint Filed on November 18,

2022 (collectively, the Dismissal Orders; the Planning

Department, the Hui, and the Charter School are collectively

referred to as Appellees); and March 4, 2024 Order Denying

[Rohr's] Motion to Reconsider or Amend [the Dismissal Orders]

(Order Denying Reconsideration).

 Rohr raises three points of error on appeal, contending

that the Circuit Court erred when it: (1) treated Appellees'

November 18, 21, and 22, 2022 Hawai#i Rules of Civil Procedure

(HRCP) Rule 12(b) motions (Motions to Dismiss) as tolling

motions; (2) dismissed the Amended Complaint under the doctrine

of primary jurisdiction; and (3) left Rohr unfairly disadvantaged

by the court's remedy.

 Upon careful review of the record and the briefs

submitted by the parties, and having given due consideration to

the arguments advanced and the issues raised, we resolve Rohr's
points of error as follows:

 (1) Rohr argues that the Circuit Court erred by

treating the Motions to Dismiss as "tolling" motions with respect

to Appellees' deadline to file an answer to the Amended

Complaint. In short, when the Circuit Court granted Rohr's

request to file an amended complaint, rather than requiring the

Appellees to file new – and likely substantially similar –

motions to dismiss the Amended Complaint, the Circuit Court

essentially kept Appellees' existing Motions to Dismiss pending

 2
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

as to Rohr's claims, and allowed them to supplement the Motions

to Dismiss, if necessary, to address the Amended Complaint.

 Rohr raised no objection to this procedure. It is

well-settled that issues not raised in the lower court will not

be considered on appeal. See, e.g., Kawamata Farms, Inc. v.

United Agri Prods., 86 Hawai#i 214, 248, 948 P.2d 1055, 1089

(1997). Accordingly, we conclude that Rohr's argument that the

Circuit Court abused its discretion in streamlining the pleadings

response process in this manner is waived.

 (2) Rohr argues that the Circuit Court erred in

applying the primary jurisdiction doctrine and dismissing the

Amended Complaint.

 Primary jurisdiction "comes into play whenever

enforcement of the claim requires the resolution of issues which,

under the regulatory scheme have been placed within the special

competence of an administrative body." Pac. Lightnet, Inc. v.

Time Warner Telecom, Inc., 131 Hawai#i 257, 268, 318 P.3d 97, 108
(2013) (cleaned up). While "conceptually analogous" to the

exhaustion of administrative remedies doctrine, the primary
jurisdiction doctrine "does not require a determination that the

court lacks jurisdiction over the matter." Id. at 268-69, 318

P.3d at 108-09 (citations omitted; emphasis in original).

"Instead, primary jurisdiction presumes that the claim at issue

is originally cognizable by both the court and the agency." Id.

at 269, 318 P.3d at 109 (emphasis in original) (citing Aged

Hawaiians v. Hawaiian Homes Comm'n, 78 Hawai#i 192, 202, 891 P.2d
279, 289 (1995)).

 3
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 Here, Rohr initiated proceedings at the agency level.

She petitioned the County of Hawai#i Board of Appeals (Board of

Appeals) on June 14, 2022, seeking reversal of the issuance of an

SMA Minor Permit to the Hui, arguing, inter alia, that the

challenged Kaumaui Project violated the General Plan, community

plan, and zoning, and therefore violated Hawaii Revised Statutes

(HRS) § 205A-26 (Supp. 2020).

 Less than three months later, before the Board of

Appeals had completed its decision-making, on September 6, 2022,

Rohr filed this suit in the Circuit Court, primarily arguing that

the SMA Minor Permit was approved without requiring the

preparation of an Environmental Assessment (EA) and, therefore,

was issued in violation of HRS chapter 343 (HEPA), Hawai#i

Administrative Rules (HAR) chapter 11-200.1, subchapter 9, and

article XI, section 9 of the Hawai#i Constitution. At that

point, the agency and the court proceedings took place alongside

one another. The Board of Appeals heard testimony concerning

Rohr's petition on September 9, and November 4, 2022. The Board

of Appeals Decision was issued on February 2, 2023. In light of

the Board of Appeals Decision, the Circuit Court orally stated at

the February 10, 2023 hearing on the Motions to Dismiss that Rohr

"can go through the proper procedures and appeal" via HRS § 91-

142 and that the court was dismissing this case without

prejudice.

 2
 Thereafter, Rohr did in fact timely file a notice of appeal from
the notice of Board of Appeals Decision.

 4
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 The primary jurisdiction doctrine applies here because,

pursuant to HRS § 343-7(a) (Supp. 2021), the circuit courts have

original jurisdiction over proceedings challenging the lack of an

EA required under HRS § 343-5 (Supp. 2021). See, e.g., Maui Lani

Neighbors, Inc. v. State, 156 Hawai#i 520, 542, 575 P.3d 610, 632

(2025).3 Under HRS § 343-7(a),4 a suit must be initiated within

120 days of the agency's decision to carry out or approve the

action, as Rohr did here, or within 120 days after the proposed

action is started if no formal determination was made. In

addition, an agency's action, including a determination not to

require an EA, is within the special competence of the

 3
 In Maui Lani Neighbors, the supreme court stated:

 HRS chapter 343 establishes a system of environmental
 review to ensure that environmental concerns are given
 appropriate consideration along with economic and technical
 considerations in decision-making processes. This allows
 for parties to challenge agency actions directly through the
 court system, as HRS § 343-7 explicitly contemplates a
 "judicial proceeding." Indeed, our courts frequently hear
 HEPA claims. See, e.g., Umberger v. Dep't of Land & Nat.
 Res., 140 Hawai#i 500, 403 P.3d 277 (2017); Kepo#o v. Kane,
 106 Hawai#i 270, 103 P.3d 939 (2005); [Citizens for Prot.
 of] N. Kohala [Coastline v. Cnty. of Hawai#i], 91 Hawai#i 94,
 979 P.2d 1120 [(1999)]. Clearly, the circuit court has
 jurisdiction to hear challenges brought pursuant to HRS
 § 343-7 given the plain language of the statute and
 extensive history of our courts hearing such cases.

 156 Hawai#i at 542, 575 P.3d at 632.

 4
 HRS § 343-7(a) provides:

 § 343-7 Limitation of actions. (a) Any judicial
 proceeding, the subject of which is the lack of assessment
 required under section 343-5, shall be initiated within one
 hundred twenty days of the agency's decision to carry out or
 approve the action, or, if a proposed action is undertaken
 without a formal determination by the agency that a
 statement is or is not required, a judicial proceeding shall
 be instituted within one hundred twenty days after the
 proposed action is started. The office, any agency
 responsible for approval of the action, or the applicant
 shall be adjudged an aggrieved party for the purposes of
 bringing judicial action under this subsection. Others, by
 environmental court action, may be adjudged aggrieved.

 5
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

administrative body issuing an SMA permit and may be challenged

through the appeals procedure set forth in HRS § 91-14, as

referenced by the Circuit Court. Thus, a HEPA claim is

originally cognizable by both the court and the agency and the

Circuit Court did not err in concluding that the primary

jurisdiction doctrine was applicable in this case.

 (3) Rohr further argues that, even if the Circuit

Court did not err in applying the primary jurisdiction doctrine,

she was unfairly disadvantaged by the court's remedy, i.e.,

dismissal of the case, as opposed to retaining jurisdiction and

staying the proceeding.

 This court has previously held:
 Where the doctrine of primary jurisdiction applies, the
 court has the "discretion either to retain jurisdiction [and
 stay the proceedings] or, if the parties would not be
 unfairly disadvantaged, to dismiss the case without
 prejudice." Reiter v. Cooper, 507 U.S. 258, 268–69, 113
 S.Ct. 1213, 1220, 122 L.Ed.2d 604 (U.S.N.C.1993).

Dancil v. Arakawa, 132 Hawai#i 472, 478, 323 P.3d 116, 122 (App.

2012).

 Rohr argues, inter alia, that "[a]ny judicial

proceeding, the subject of which is the lack of assessment
required under section 343-5, shall be initiated within one

hundred twenty days of the agency's decision to carry out or

approve the action;" however, that period "expired before the

Board of Appeals acted on Rohr's Petition for an appeal of the

Planning Director's decision to issue the SMA minor permit."

This argument has merit. The SMA Minor Permit was issued to the

Hui on June 6, 2022. Rohr petitioned the Board of Appeals on

June 14, 2022. The Board of Appeals Decision was not issued

until February 2, 2023. Had Rohr waited until the Board of

 6
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Appeals promulgated its decision, the statute of limitations for

her claims would have run pursuant to HRS § 343-7(a).

 The Planning Department argues that the running of a

statute of limitations is not per se an unfair disadvantage.

Both the Planning Department and the Hui argue that Rohr could

have raised the HEPA issue in her petition to the Board of

Appeals, but chose not to do so. Regarding the latter argument,

HRS § 343-7(a) expressly provides for a judicial action and the

Appellees provide no authority for the proposition that the

statutory right of action is foreclosed if the issue could have

been raised in an agency proceeding. Regarding the former

argument, under the circumstances of this case, we conclude that

Rohr was in fact disadvantaged by the dismissal of the Circuit

Court action "without prejudice," as prejudice effectively

attached when the case was dismissed because any newly filed suit

would be untimely under HRS § 343-7(a). See generally Fratinardo

v. Emps.' Ret. Sys. of State of Haw., 121 Hawai#i 462, 469, 220
P.3d 1043, 1050 (App. 2009) (noting federal cases finding that

the running of a statute of limitations constitutes a
disadvantage). Presumably, Appellees will at least argue that

HRS chapter 91 review of Rohr's HEPA challenge is waived in the

agency appeal because she did not raise it in her initial

petition to the Board of Appeals. Accordingly, we conclude that

the Circuit Court's dismissal, rather than the staying of Rohr'

(1997). Accordingly, we conclude that Rohr's argument that the

Circuit Court abused its discretion in streamlining the pleadings

response process in this manner is waived.

 (2) Rohr argues that the Circuit Court erred in

applying the primary jurisdiction doctrine and dismissing the

Amended Complaint.

 Primary jurisdiction "comes into play whenever

enforcement of the claim requires the resolution of issues which,

under the regulatory scheme have been placed within the special

competence of an administrative body." Pac. Lightnet, Inc. v.
Time Warner Telecom, Inc., 131 Hawai#i 257, 268, 318 P.3d 97, 108

(2013) (cleaned up). While "conceptually analogous" to the

exhaustion of administrative remedies doctrine, the primary
jurisdiction doctrine "does not require a determination that the

court lacks jurisdiction over the matter." Id. at 268-69, 318

P.3d at 108-09 (citations omitted; emphasis in original).

"Instead, primary jurisdiction presumes that the claim at issue

is originally cognizable by both the court and the agency." Id.

at 269, 318 P.3d at 109 (emphasis in original) (citing Aged

Hawaiians v. Hawaiian Homes Comm'n, 78 Hawai#i 192, 202, 891 P.2d

279, 289 (1995)).

 3
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 Here, Rohr initiated proceedings at the agency level.

She petitioned the County of Hawai#i Board of Appeals (Board of

Appeals) on June 14, 2022, seeking reversal of the issuance of an

SMA Minor Permit to the Hui, arguing, inter alia, that the

challenged Kaumaui Project violated the General Plan, community

plan, and zoning, and therefore violated Hawaii Revised Statutes

(HRS) § 205A-26 (Supp. 2020).

 Less than three months later, before the Board of

Appeals had completed its decision-making, on September 6, 2022,

Rohr filed this suit in the Circuit Court, primarily arguing that

the SMA Minor Permit was approved without requiring the

preparation of an Environmental Assessment (EA) and, therefore,

was issued in violation of HRS chapter 343 (HEPA), Hawai#i

Administrative Rules (HAR) chapter 11-200.1, subchapter 9, and

article XI, section 9 of the Hawai#i Constitution. At that

point, the agency and the court proceedings took place alongside

one another. The Board of Appeals heard testimony concerning

Rohr's petition on September 9, and November 4, 2022. The Board

of Appeals Decision was issued on February 2, 2023. In light of

the Board of Appeals Decision, the Circuit Court orally stated at

the February 10, 2023 hearing on the Motions to Dismiss that Rohr

"can go through the proper procedures and appeal" via HRS § 91-

142 and that the court was dismissing this case without

prejudice.

 2
 Thereafter, Rohr did in fact timely file a notice of appeal from
the notice of Board of Appeals Decision.

 4
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 The primary jurisdiction doctrine applies here because,

pursuant to HRS § 343-7(a) (Supp. 2021), the circuit courts have

original jurisdiction over proceedings challenging the lack of an

EA required under HRS § 343-5 (Supp. 2021). See, e.g., Maui Lani

Neighbors, Inc. v. State, 156 Hawai#i 520, 542, 575 P.3d 610, 632

(2025).3 Under HRS § 343-7(a),4 a suit must be initiated within

120 days of the agency's decision to carry out or approve the

action, as Rohr did here, or within 120 days after the proposed

action is started if no formal determination was made. In

addition, an agency's action, including a determination not to

require an EA, is within the special competence of the

 3
 In Maui Lani Neighbors, the supreme court stated:

 HRS chapter 343 establishes a system of environmental
 review to ensure that environmental concerns are given
 appropriate consideration along with economic and technical
 considerations in decision-making processes. This allows
 for parties to challenge agency actions directly through the
 court system, as HRS § 343-7 explicitly contemplates a
 "judicial proceeding." Indeed, our courts frequently hear
 HEPA claims. See, e.g., Umberger v. Dep't of Land & Nat.
 Res., 140 Hawai#i 500, 403 P.3d 277 (2017); Kepo#o v. Kane,
 106 Hawai#i 270, 103 P.3d 939 (2005); [Citizens for Prot.
 of] N. Kohala [Coastline v. Cnty. of Hawai#i], 91 Hawai#i 94,
 979 P.2d 1120 [(1999)]. Clearly, the circuit court has
 jurisdiction to hear challenges brought pursuant to HRS
 § 343-7 given the plain language of the statute and
 extensive history of our courts hearing such cases.

 156 Hawai#i at 542, 575 P.3d at 632.

 4
 HRS § 343-7(a) provides:

 § 343-7 Limitation of actions. (a) Any judicial
 proceeding, the subject of which is the lack of assessment
 required under section 343-5, shall be initiated within one
 hundred twenty days of the agency's decision to carry out or
 approve the action, or, if a proposed action is undertaken
 without a formal determination by the agency that a
 statement is or is not required, a judicial proceeding shall
 be instituted within one hundred twenty days after the
 proposed action is started. The office, any agency
 responsible for approval of the action, or the applicant
 shall be adjudged an aggrieved party for the purposes of
 bringing judicial action under this subsection. Others, by
 environmental court action, may be adjudged aggrieved.

 5
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

administrative body issuing an SMA permit and may be challenged

through the appeals procedure set forth in HRS § 91-14, as

referenced by the Circuit Court. Thus, a HEPA claim is

originally cognizable by both the court and the agency and the

Circuit Court did not err in concluding that the primary

jurisdiction doctrine was applicable in this case.

 (3) Rohr further argues that, even if the Circuit

Court did not err in applying the primary jurisdiction doctrine,

she was unfairly disadvantaged by the court's remedy, i.e.,

dismissal of the case, as opposed to retaining jurisdiction and

staying the proceeding.

 This court has previously held:
 Where the doctrine of primary jurisdiction applies, the
 court has the "discretion either to retain jurisdiction [and
 stay the proceedings] or, if the parties would not be
 unfairly disadvantaged, to dismiss the case without
 prejudice." Reiter v. Cooper, 507 U.S. 258, 268–69, 113
 S.Ct. 1213, 1220, 122 L.Ed.2d 604 (U.S.N.C.1993).

Dancil v. Arakawa, 132 Hawai#i 472, 478, 323 P.3d 116, 122 (App.

2012).

 Rohr argues, inter alia, that "[a]ny judicial

proceeding, the subject of which is the lack of assessment
required under section 343-5, shall be initiated within one

hundred twenty days of the agency's decision to carry out or

approve the action;" however, that period "expired before the

Board of Appeals acted on Rohr's Petition for an appeal of the

Planning Director's decision to issue the SMA minor permit."

This argument has merit. The SMA Minor Permit was issued to the

Hui on June 6, 2022. Rohr petitioned the Board of Appeals on

June 14, 2022. The Board of Appeals Decision was not issued

until February 2, 2023. Had Rohr waited until the Board of

 6
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAI#I REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Appeals promulgated its decision, the statute of limitations for

her claims would have run pursuant to HRS § 343-7(a).

 The Planning Department argues that the running of a

statute of limitations is not per se an unfair disadvantage.

Both the Planning Department and the Hui argue that Rohr could

have raised the HEPA issue in her petition to the Board of

Appeals, but chose not to do so. Regarding the latter argument,

HRS § 343-7(a) expressly provides for a judicial action and the

Appellees provide no authority for the proposition that the

statutory right of action is foreclosed if the issue could have

been raised in an agency proceeding. Regarding the former

argument, under the circumstances of this case, we conclude that

Rohr was in fact disadvantaged by the dismissal of the Circuit

Court action "without prejudice," as prejudice effectively

attached when the case was dismissed because any newly filed suit

would be untimely under HRS § 343-7(a). See generally Fratinardo
v. Emps.' Ret. Sys. of State of Haw., 121 Hawai#i 462, 469, 220

P.3d 1043, 1050 (App. 2009) (noting federal cases finding that

the running of a statute of limitations constitutes a
disadvantage). Presumably, Appellees will at least argue that

HRS chapter 91 review of Rohr's HEPA challenge is waived in the

agency appeal because she did not raise it in her initial

petition to the Board of Appeals. Accordingly, we conclude that

the Circuit Court's dismissal, rather than the staying of Rohr

NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 Electronically Filed
 Intermediate Court of Appeals
 CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX
 30-OCT-2026
 07:59 AM
 Dkt. 282 SO

 NO. CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX

 IN THE INTERMEDIATE COURT OF APPEALS

 OF THE STATE OF HAWAIʻI

 ASSOCIATION OF APARTMENT OWNERS OF KUHIO SHORES AT POIPU,
 Plaintiff-Appellee,
 v.
 WILLIAM H. GILLIAM, Defendant-Appellant, and
PACIFIC RIM PROPERTY SERVICE CORPORATION, A HAWAIʻI CORPORATION;
 Defendant/Counterclaim Plaintiff-Appellee, and DIRECTOR OF
 FINANCE, COUNTY OF KAUAʻI, Defendant-Appellee, and JOHN DOES 1-
10, JANE DOES, 1-10, DOE PARTNERSHIPS 1-10, DOE CORPORATIONS 1-
 10, DOE ENTITIES 1-10, AND DOE GOVERNMENTAL UNITS 1-10,
 Defendants.

 APPEAL FROM THE CIRCUIT COURT OF THE FIFTH CIRCUIT
 (CIVIL NO. 5CC161000063)

 SUMMARY DISPOSITION ORDER
 (By: Nakasone, Chief Judge, Wadsworth and Gluck, JJ.)
 Self-represented Defendant-Appellant William Gilliam
(Gilliam) appeals from the October 20, 2025 "Order Granting
Amended Receiver's Motion for Instructions Regarding Sale of
Property" (Order) and accompanying "Writ of Possession" (Writ)
issued by the Circuit Court of the Fifth Circuit (Circuit
Court). 1 Gilliam alleges that the Circuit Court improperly
granted the Order and Writ against him and

 1 The Honorable Randal G.B. Valenciano entered the Order and Writ.
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Defendant/Counterclaim Plaintiff-Appellee Pacific Rim Property
Service Corporation (PR1).
 Gilliam raises the following seven points of error on
appeal: 2 (1) "the [Circuit Court] lack[ed] jurisdiction by
service of process on any defendant"; (2) "the [Circuit Court]
lack[ed] subject matter jurisdiction [over] a claim to foreclose
a lien against a non-member"; (3) unclean hands; (4) "[an]
action for a receiver under [Hawai‘i Revised Statutes
(HRS)] § 414-422 is a special proceeding"; (5) "the court abused
its discretion by fail[ing] to stay pursuant to the special
motion to dismiss"; (6) "there is no issue preclusion"; and
(7) "the hearing on []September 23rd on the amended motion
improperly admitted hearsay [evidence] . . . and . . .
[disallowed] testimony [resulting in] a denial of due process."
 Upon careful review of the record and the briefs
submitted by the parties and having given due consideration to
the arguments advanced and the issues raised, we affirm.
 I. BACKGROUND
 At its core, this case is about ownership of a
condominium: Unit 209 of the Condominium Project, Kuhio Shores
at Poipu (Property). For many years, Gilliam has argued that he
owns the Property. He does not.
 In 2009, the Property was owned by PR1, a corporation.
Gilliam's mother, Vivian T. Lord (Lord), was the sole officer
and director of PR1. Lord passed away on June 6, 2009.

 2 Gilliam does not include a points of error section as required by
Hawaiʻi Rules of Appellate Procedure (HRAP) Rule 28(b)(4) (eff. 2022). As
such, his intended points of error and arguments are hard to discern. The
following points of error are taken from Gilliam's Opening Brief's section
headers. Where possible, we have tried to address each of Gilliam's numerous
arguments consistent with this court's "policy of affording litigants the
opportunity to have their cases heard on the merits, where possible." Morgan
v. Plan. Dep't, Cnty. of Kauai, 104 Hawaiʻi 173, 180-81, 86 P.3d 982, 989-90
(2004) (citation and internal quotation signals omitted).

 2
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 On April 28, 2016, the Association of Apartment Owners
of Kuhio Shores at Poipu (AOAO) filed a Complaint for
Foreclosure (Complaint) against PR1, Lord, and the Director of
Finance, County of Kaua‘i. The AOAO alleged PR1 and/or Lord were
the owner(s) of the Property and failed to pay various
assessments and fees.
 On April 27, 2017, Gilliam filed a Motion to Dismiss
the Complaint (2017 MTD), ostensibly on behalf of the
corporation that owned the Property ("Pacific Rim Property
Services Corporation"). 3 But "Pacific Rim Property Services
Corporation" (again, referred to herein as PR1) no longer
existed. Instead, Gilliam had incorporated a new entity with
the same name (referred to herein as PR2) with himself as its
sole officer and director.
 The AOAO filed a Memorandum in Opposition to the 2017
MTD, asserting that the Department of Commerce and Consumer
Affairs of the State of Hawai‘i records showed: (1) Lord was
PR1's sole officer and director; (2) Lord passed away on June 6,
2009; (3) PR1 was involuntarily dissolved on December 4, 2012;
and (4) Gilliam incorporated a new corporation with the same
name (again, PR2) on December 2, 2013, with Gilliam acting as
its sole officer and director. The AOAO asserted that it had no
information indicating that title of the Property had been
transferred from PR1. On August 15, 2017, the Circuit Court
granted in part and denied in part the 2017 MTD. 4

 3 From the record, it appears that Gilliam retained counsel to
represent PR1; however, Gilliam had (and has) no interest in PR1.

 4 The Circuit Court granted the motion as to attorneys' fees
imposed as a sanction against the AOAO for violating Rule 12 of the Rules of
the Circuit Courts of the State of Hawaiʻi.

 The Honorable Kathleen N.A. Watanabe entered the order granting
in part and denying in part the 2017 MTD.

 3
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 On June 26, 2018, the AOAO filed "Plaintiff [AOAO]'s
Motion for Appointment of Receiver" (Motion for Receiver). The
AOAO argued that PR1 was still the owner of the Property and
that a receiver was necessary to settle the unfinished business
of the corporation. Gilliam filed an opposition to the Motion
for Receiver — again, supposedly on behalf of PR1 — and argued
that he was a shareholder of PR1 at the time of Lord's death and
at the time of PR1's dissolution. Gilliam also claimed that he
inherited his mother's shares of PR1 upon her passing, such that
the Property had passed to him as the sole owner of the
corporation upon its dissolution.
 On October 19, 2018, the Circuit Court entered its
"Order Granting Plaintiff [AOAO]'s Motion for Appointment of
Receiver" (Order Appointing Receiver) and appointed George R.
Robinson (Robinson) as receiver for PR1. Robinson was tasked
with "assisting in all acts that are necessary for the final
settlement of the unfinished business of [PR1]" including
"determining the legal owner of the [Property]."
 On March 27, 2019, Robinson filed his Receiver Report.
Among other things, Robinson reported that Gilliam was "not
paying the real property taxes on the property and continuing to
rent the property out as a vacation rental." Robinson asked
that the Circuit Court approve his report, convert the matter to
a court-ordered sale of the Property, and grant him the
authority to complete the sale.
 On August 19, 2019, Gilliam filed for Chapter 11
bankruptcy — ostensibly on behalf of PR1. In re Pac. Rim Prop.
Serv. Corp., No. BAP HI-20-1071-BTL, 2020 WL 4371106, at *2
(B.A.P. 9th Cir. July 29, 2020). The Bankruptcy Court dismissed
the case. Id. at *2. The AOAO moved to annul the automatic
stay imposed by the bankruptcy proceeding, and the Bankruptcy
Court granted the motion. Id. Gilliam appealed the Bankruptcy

 4
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Court's annulment of the stay. Id. On appeal, the United
States Bankruptcy Appellate Panel of the Ninth Circuit held that
Gilliam did not have standing to challenge the annulment of the
stay. Id. at *3 (concluding that "Gilliam is not a shareholder,
much less the sole shareholder, of [PR1]" and that "[Gilliam]
has not identified any particularized or concrete injury arising
from the bankruptcy court's order annulling the stay of [PR1].
Gilliam is not [PR1], nor does he have any interest in or
control over [PR1] or its assets, including the [Property]").
 On October 2, 2019, the Circuit Court issued an "Order
Granting Plaintiff [AOAO]'s Motion for Instructions for the
Receiver" (2019 Order) and a "Writ of Possession" (2019 Writ)
for the Property. The 2019 Order directed the Receiver to sell
the Property to settle the debts of PR1. On November 1, 2019,
Gilliam appealed the 2019 Order and 2019 Writ.
 On October 25, 2019, Gilliam filed for Chapter 13
bankruptcy on behalf of himself, contending that the Property
was part of his bankruptcy estate. In re Gilliam, No. CV 20-
00194 JMS-WRP, 2020 WL 5848340, at *1 (D. Haw. Oct. 1, 2020),
aff'd, 859 F. App'x 832 (9th Cir. 2021). The Bankruptcy Court,
however, found that PR1 — not Gilliam — was the owner. Id. On
appeal, the United States District Court affirmed the Bankruptcy
Court's rulings and ruled that "[t]he Bankruptcy Court's factual
finding—that the condominium was not property of Gilliam's
estate—was not clearly erroneous, and is well-supported by ample
evidence in the record." Id. at *5.
 On April 17, 2024, this court ruled on the appeal of
the 2019 Order and 2019 Writ, vacating both and remanding for
further proceedings. Ass'n of Apartment Owners of Kuhio Shores
at Poipu v. Pac. Rim Prop. Serv. Corp., No. CAAP-XX-XXXXXXX,
2024 WL 1656266, at *2-3 (App. Apr. 17, 2024) (SDO). This court
concluded that although Gilliam was personally named in the 2019

 5
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

Order and the 2019 Writ, Gilliam was never made a party to the
action (2024 Order). Id. at *2.
 On remand, on November 27, 2024, the AOAO filed its
First Amended Complaint for Foreclosure (FAC), adding Gilliam as
a defendant.
 On January 13, 2025, Gilliam filed a Motion to
Dismiss. The Circuit Court denied the motion. Gilliam then
filed various documents, including a Special Motion to Dismiss
(SMTD). The SMTD asserted that the FAC was a "SLAPP" action but
did not explain how or why, other than noting that the AOAO had
previously "slapped" the Property's common expense assessment
account with false entries. On March 12, 2025, the Circuit
Court denied the SMTD. 5
 Nine days later (on March 21, 2025), Robinson filed
"Receiver's Motion for Instructions Regarding Sale of Property"
and an "Amended Receiver's Motion for Instructions Regarding
Sale of Property" (Motion for Instructions). Gilliam filed an
"Opposition to Motion Writ of Possession & to Sell" (Opposition
to Motion for Instructions) arguing that the Circuit Court
should deny the Motion for Instructions. Gilliam then
unsuccessfully sought to remove the case to federal court,
delaying proceedings by several more months.
 On August 12, 2025, Gilliam filed an Answer and
Counterclaim to the FAC.
 On September 23, 2025, the Circuit Court held a
hearing on the Motion for Instructions and orally granted the
motion. This appeal followed.

 5 On March 28, 2025 — sixteen days after the Circuit Court had
ruled on the SMTD — Gilliam filed his Memorandum in Support of Special Motion
to Dismiss. This memorandum set forth arguments regarding the application of
HRS chapter 634G to his claim, among other things. The Circuit Court's March
12, 2025 order denying the SMTD did not address HRS chapter 634G, however,
because Gilliam had not raised the issue in his motion.

 6
  NOT FOR PUBLICATION IN WEST'S HAWAIʻI REPORTS AND PACIFIC REPORTER

 II. DISCUSSION
 A. Ownership of the Property and Issue Preclusion
 At the outset, many of Gilliam's arguments are made on
behalf of PR1 or are based on his claimed ownership interest in
the Property. In Gilliam's sixth point of error, which we
address first, it appears that Gilliam argues the bankruptcy
decisions do not preclude him from claiming an interest in PR1
or the Property. He seems to argue that because one of the
bankruptcy cases was dismissed, and because this court
previously remanded this case, the Order Appointing Receiver has
been invalidated. Gilliam's arguments lack merit.
 First, the Order Appointing Receiver was not
invalidated by this court's previous ruling. This court vacated
